chapters.title: Unit 8: Women's Role in the Pakistan Movement

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Do men and women have different roles in the society, community and at home? How?
    Ans: Men and women share many duties but often play different roles. At home, women commonly manage the house and raise children while men commonly earn for the family, but both support each other. In society and the community, both men and women work as teachers, doctors, workers and leaders, and the lesson shows that in the Pakistan Movement women worked side by side with men as equal partners.
  • Q: What is the role of women in the development of a country?
    Ans: Women are half of the population, so no country can progress without them, as Quaid-e-Azam said: 'No nation can make any progress without the cooperation of its women.' Women develop a country by educating children, working in every field, and taking part in public life. In the Pakistan Movement they organised, mobilised and even led processions, which helped create Pakistan.

Comprehension A. Answer the following questions

  • Q: 1. How did Quaid-e-Azam empower and emancipate the Muslim women of the Sub-Continent?
    Ans: Quaid-e-Azam brought about a social revolution in the emancipation and empowerment of Muslim women. He repeatedly stressed that women must be equal partners of men, kept Fatima Jinnah visibly at his side in all political activities, and at the Patna session in 1938 created the All India Muslim Women's Sub-Committee of the Muslim League. Through it, women came out of their homes, organised and mobilised other women, and became activists and parliamentarians.
  • Q: 2. How did Begum Fatima, the principal of Jinnah Islamia College, mobilise female students?
    Ans: Begum Fatima, founder principal of the Jinnah Islamia College for girls in Lahore, played a key role in mobilising female students for the Muslim League. She invited Quaid-e-Azam to come and address the students of her college in November 1942. His declaration that no nation can progress without the cooperation of its women deeply impressed the young minds and drew the girl students into the Pakistan Movement.
  • Q: 3. Why did the Quaid-e-Azam stress the importance of women as equal partners of men in the creation of a separate homeland for Muslims?
    Ans: Quaid-e-Azam stressed this because he believed the Muslims of India could achieve the dream of a separate homeland only with the full strength of the whole nation, and women are half of it. He said no nation can make any progress without the cooperation of its women, and that if Muslim women supported their men, as they did in the days of the Prophet of Islam, the goal would soon be realised.
  • Q: 4. Describe the role of women in the Pakistan Movement, highlighting their love and aspirations for the new homeland.
    Ans: Women moved from secluded homes into the front line of the movement: Bi Amma led during the Khilafat Movement; Fatima Jinnah stood beside the Quaid; leaders like Jahanara Shahnawaz, Begum Salma Tassaduq Hussain, Begum Fatima, Shaista Ikramullah, Zari Sarfraz and Lady Abdullah Haroon organised and mobilised women in cities and districts. Girl students travelled even to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, women Leaguers held massive demonstrations in Punjab in 1946, a thousand burqa-clad women attended the Frontier Women's session at Peshawar in February 1947, and one young woman climbed the Punjab Secretariat, removed the Union Jack and hoisted the Pakistani flag. Their love of the new homeland was so deep that they braved social conservatism and police action to win a free country for their children.
  • Q: 5. Analyse the third paragraph of the lesson 'Women's Role in the Pakistan Movement' and identify the sentences that support the main idea through cause and effect.
    Ans: The third paragraph (in the printed order of the lesson, the paragraph beginning 'However, the real game changer was the Muslim League session at Patna in 1938') has the main idea that the creation of the Women's Sub-Committee brought women into the leadership of the Muslim League. Cause-and-effect support: because Quaid-e-Azam created the All India Muslim Women's Sub-Committee in 1938 (cause), by the mid-40s a galaxy of women had emerged in leadership roles (effect); and because these leaders organised and mobilised women workers in the cities and at district level (cause), women across India joined the movement in large numbers (effect).
  • Q: 6. What ideas and issues have been explored in the fifth paragraph of the text, 'Women's Role in the Pakistan Movement'.
    Ans: The fifth paragraph (the paragraph about Begum Fatima and the girl students) explores the idea that students and young women were a decisive force in the movement. It raises the issue of mobilising female students despite social conservatism, shows Begum Fatima using her college to bring students to the League, and presents Quaid-e-Azam's view, given at the college in November 1942, that national progress is impossible without women's cooperation.

Comprehension B. Choose the correct option

  • Q: 1. “Most of the Muslim women led secluded lives within their homes”. By using contextual clues the word closest in meaning to 'secluded' is __________.
    Options: involved little in outside social activities / involved too much in activities outside their homes / banned to take part in social activities / prohibited by law to take part in social activities
    Ans: involved little in outside social activities
  • Q: 2. “By the mid-40s, a galaxy of women had emerged in the leadership role of Muslim League”. In this sentence the word 'galaxy' means _______________.
    Options: a group of impressive persons / a system of numerous stars / a cluster of bright heavenly bodies. / community of people
    Ans: a group of impressive persons
  • Q: 3. “It was Quaid-e-Azam who brought about social revolution in the emancipation and empowerment of women”. In this sentence the word 'social revolution' means __________.
    Options: communal revolt / societal change / social disorders / economical change
    Ans: societal change
  • Q: 4. After reading the lesson, 'Women's Role in the Pakistan Movement', it is inferred that the role of women expanded because of ______________.
    Options: Bi- Amma speeches to khilafat gatherings. / Fatima Jinnah participation in all the activities of Quaid-e-Azam / Quaid-e-Azam who stressed the importance of Women as equal partner of men in the struggle for a separate homeland. / Begum Fatima who invited Quaid-e-Azam to address the girl student of her college.
    Ans: Quaid-e-Azam who stressed the importance of Women as equal partner of men in the struggle for a separate homeland.
  • Q: 5. After reading the lesson, 'Women's Role in the Pakistan Movement', it can be concluded that the paragraphs are arranged in_______________.
    Options: chronological order / general to specific / specific to general / spatial order
    Ans: chronological order

mcqs.q: “Most of the Muslim women led secluded lives within their homes”. By using contextual clues the word closest in meaning to 'secluded' is __________.
options: involved little in outside social activities
involved too much in activities outside their homes
banned to take part in social activities
prohibited by law to take part in social activities
mcqs.why: Secluded lives within their homes means the women were involved little in outside social activities.

mcqs.q: “By the mid-40s, a galaxy of women had emerged in the leadership role of Muslim League”. In this sentence the word 'galaxy' means _______________.
options: a cluster of bright heavenly bodies.
mcqs.why: Here 'galaxy' is used figuratively for a group of impressive persons who had emerged as women leaders by the mid-40s.

mcqs.q: “It was Quaid-e-Azam who brought about social revolution in the emancipation and empowerment of women”. In this sentence the word 'social revolution' means __________.
mcqs.why: A social revolution in this context means a great societal change in the position and empowerment of women.

mcqs.q: After reading the lesson, 'Women's Role in the Pakistan Movement', it is inferred that the role of women expanded because of ______________.
options: Bi- Amma speeches to khilafat gatherings.
Fatima Jinnah participation in all the activities of Quaid-e-Azam
Begum Fatima who invited Quaid-e-Azam to address the girl student of her college.
Quaid-e-Azam who stressed the importance of Women as equal partner of men in the struggle for a separate homeland.
mcqs.why: The lesson infers that women's role expanded because Quaid-e-Azam stressed their importance as equal partners of men in the struggle.

mcqs.q: After reading the lesson, 'Women's Role in the Pakistan Movement', it can be concluded that the paragraphs are arranged in_______________.
mcqs.why: The paragraphs move through events in time order, from the early twentieth century to 1947, so they are in chronological order.

mcqs.q: How did Quaid-e-Azam bring women into the Muslim League's work at the Patna session in 1938?
options: He opened a college for girls in Lahore
He led a demonstration in Punjab in 1946
He created the All India Muslim Women's Sub-Committee of the Muslim League
He addressed students at Jinnah Islamia College
mcqs.why: At the Patna session in 1938 Quaid-e-Azam created the All India Muslim Women's Sub-Committee, through which women organised and mobilised others.

mcqs.q: How did Begum Fatima mobilise the female students of Jinnah Islamia College?
options: She led them in a procession to Peshawar
She sent them to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa districts
She hoisted the Pakistani flag in Lahore
She invited Quaid-e-Azam to address the students in November 1942
mcqs.why: Begum Fatima invited Quaid-e-Azam to address her college students in November 1942, and his words drew them into the movement.

mcqs.q: What did the young woman do at the Punjab Secretariat, according to the lesson?
options: She removed the Union Jack and hoisted the Pakistani flag
She addressed a session of a thousand women
She organised women workers in the districts
She stood beside Quaid-e-Azam at Patna
mcqs.why: The lesson records that one young woman climbed the Punjab Secretariat, removed the Union Jack and hoisted the Pakistani flag.

mcqs.q: How many burqa-clad women attended the Frontier Women's session at Peshawar in February 1947?
mcqs.why: The solved answers state that a thousand burqa-clad women attended the Frontier Women's session at Peshawar in February 1947.

mcqs.q: According to Quaid-e-Azam, why could no nation progress without its women?
options: Women are half of the population and national progress needs their cooperation
Women should stay in secluded homes only
Women only raise children at home
Men alone cannot work in any field
mcqs.why: Quaid-e-Azam said no nation can make any progress without the cooperation of its women, who are half of the population.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary: By using your knowledge of the meaning of common roots, try to find out the meaning of the following words

  • Q: automatic
    Ans: Root 'auto' means self. Automatic means working by itself, without direct human control (as in the book's examples: automatic, autobiography).
  • Q: anti-war
    Ans: Root 'anti' means against. Anti-war means against war, opposed to war (as in the book's examples: antibiotics, antidote).
  • Q: dispel
    Ans: Root 'pel / pul' means push / drive. Dispel means to drive away and make (a doubt, feeling, or belief) disappear, as given in the glossary of this lesson.
  • Q: aqueous
    Ans: Root 'aqua' means water. Aqueous means containing water, or made of / like water (as in the book's examples: aquarium, aquatic).
  • Q: astrology
    Ans: Root 'ast(er)' means star. Astrology means the study of the positions of the stars and planets and their supposed effect on people's lives (as in the book's examples: asteroid, astronomy, astronaut).

Grammar A. Rewrite the complete sentence using the adverb in brackets in its usual position

  • Q: 1. I must see a dentist. (also)
    Ans: I must also see a dentist.
  • Q: 2. I was joking. (only)
    Ans: I was only joking.
  • Q: 3. Did you enjoy the film? (both)
    Ans: Did you both enjoy the film?
  • Q: 4. Javeria watches TV. (hardly)
    Ans: Javeria hardly watches TV.
  • Q: 5. She drives her car. (carefully)
    Ans: She drives her car carefully.

Grammar B. Form adverbs from these adjectives

  • Q: perfect
    Ans: perfectly
  • Q: late
    Ans: late
  • Q: quick
    Ans: quickly
  • Q: regular
    Ans: regularly
  • Q: nice
    Ans: nicely
  • Q: terrible
    Ans: terribly
  • Q: heavy
    Ans: heavily
  • Q: good
    Ans: well
  • Q: hard
    Ans: hard
  • Q: fantastic
    Ans: fantastically
  • Q: quiet
    Ans: quietly
  • Q: recent
    Ans: recently

Grammar C. Complete the sentence using an adjective or adverb

  • Q: 1. He's always in a rush. I don't understand why he walks so ____ (hurry/hurriedly).
    Ans: hurriedly
  • Q: 2. I prefer studying in the library. It's always ____ (quiet/quietly).
    Ans: quiet
  • Q: 3. Masood ____ (happy/happily) took the assistant job. He had been looking for a position all summer.
    Ans: happily
  • Q: 4. They speak Pashto very ____ (good/well). They lived in Peshawar for two years.
    Ans: well
  • Q: 5. Please be ____ (careful/carefully) in the hallway. The walls have just been painted.
    Ans: careful

Grammar D. Fill in the blank with the correct comparative / superlative form of the adverb (in parentheses)

  • Q: 1. We walked ____ than the rest of the people. (slowly)
    Ans: more slowly
  • Q: 2. The man drove ____ than last time. (far)
    Ans: farther
  • Q: 3. They called us ____ in the afternoon. (late)
    Ans: later
  • Q: 4. The work went ____ today because all the workers showed up. (good)
    Ans: better
  • Q: 5. My mother and my sister talked ____ than the other guests. (loudly)
    Ans: more loudly

Grammar E. Underline the adverb phrases in the following sentences

  • Q: 1. We hurried down the street to catch the bus.
    Ans: Adverb phrases: down the street (where); to catch the bus (why - purpose).
  • Q: 2. She was born on the very same day as her friend.
    Ans: Adverb phrase: on the very same day as her friend (when).
  • Q: 3. Asad fell asleep holding his book.
    Ans: Adverb phrase: holding his book (how).
  • Q: 4. Every now and then they meet and chat.
    Ans: Adverb phrase: Every now and then (when / how often).
  • Q: 5. For now, I would like to ask you to leave.
    Ans: Adverb phrase: For now (when).

Grammar F. Underline the adverb clause in the following sentences

  • Q: 1. Whether you like it or not, you have to go to bed now.
    Ans: Adverb clause: Whether you like it or not (concession).
  • Q: 2. Unless you run fast, you will miss the bus.
    Ans: Adverb clause: Unless you run fast (condition).
  • Q: 3. Once they saw the car coming, the birds flew away from the street.
    Ans: Adverb clause: Once they saw the car coming (time).
  • Q: 4. Although she has a business degree, she is working as a clerk.
    Ans: Adverb clause: Although she has a business degree (concession).
  • Q: 5. You must keep practicing the math question until you get it right.
    Ans: Adverb clause: until you get it right (time).
  • Q: 6. Give us a call when you get back from your trip.
    Ans: Adverb clause: when you get back from your trip (time).
  • Q: 7. Since I'll be working late, I'll eat dinner in the office.
    Ans: Adverb clause: Since I'll be working late (reason).
  • Q: 8. The fireworks show will start after the sun goes down.
    Ans: Adverb clause: after the sun goes down (time).
  • Q: 9. Whenever you promise to do something, you need to keep it.
    Ans: Adverb clause: Whenever you promise to do something (time).

mcqs.q: Rewrite with the adverb in its usual position: 'I must see a dentist. (also)'
options: I must also see a dentist
I also must see a dentist only
Also I must see a dentist today
I must see also a dentist
mcqs.why: The solved sentence places 'also' after 'must': 'I must also see a dentist.'

mcqs.q: Rewrite with the adverb in its usual position: 'I was joking. (only)'
mcqs.why: The solved sentence places 'only' before the verb form it qualifies: 'I was only joking.'

mcqs.q: Rewrite with the adverb in its usual position: 'Javeria watches TV. (hardly)'
mcqs.why: The adverb 'hardly' goes before the main verb, giving 'Javeria hardly watches TV.'

mcqs.q: What is the adverb formed from the adjective 'perfect'?
mcqs.why: Adding -ly to 'perfect' forms the adverb 'perfectly', as given in the adverb-formation exercise.

mcqs.q: What is the adverb formed from the adjective 'good'?
mcqs.why: The adverb form of 'good' is the irregular adverb 'well', as in speaking a language well.

mcqs.q: What is the adverb form of the adjective 'hard' in this exercise?
mcqs.why: In the exercise the adverb form of 'hard' stays 'hard' itself, unlike 'hardly' which has a different meaning.

mcqs.q: Complete: 'He's always in a rush. I don't understand why he walks so ____ (hurry/hurriedly).'
mcqs.why: An adverb is needed to describe how he walks, so the correct choice is 'hurriedly', not the noun or verb 'hurry'.

mcqs.q: Complete: 'I prefer studying in the library. It's always ____ (quiet/quietly).'
mcqs.why: After 'is', an adjective describing the library is needed, so the correct choice is 'quiet'.

mcqs.q: Complete: 'Masood ____ (happy/happily) took the assistant job.'
mcqs.why: An adverb is needed to describe how Masood took the job, so the correct choice is 'happily'.

mcqs.q: Complete: 'Please be ____ (careful/carefully) in the hallway. The walls have just been painted.'
mcqs.why: After 'be', an adjective describing the person is needed, so the correct choice is 'careful'.

mcqs.q: Complete with the comparative adverb: 'We walked ____ than the rest of the people. (slowly)'
mcqs.why: The comparative form of the adverb 'slowly' is 'more slowly', used with 'than' in the sentence.

mcqs.q: Complete with the correct form: 'The work went ____ today because all the workers showed up. (good)'
mcqs.why: The comparative adverb form of 'good / well' is 'better', so the work went better today.

mcqs.q: In 'We hurried down the street to catch the bus', the adverb phrase 'down the street' tells us:
mcqs.why: The exercise identifies 'down the street' as the adverb phrase telling where, while 'to catch the bus' tells why.

mcqs.q: In 'Every now and then they meet and chat', the adverb phrase 'Every now and then' tells us:
options: when or how often they meet
mcqs.why: The exercise identifies 'Every now and then' as an adverb phrase of time, telling when or how often they meet.

mcqs.q: In 'Unless you run fast, you will miss the bus', the adverb clause 'Unless you run fast' expresses:
mcqs.why: The exercise identifies 'Unless you run fast' as an adverb clause of condition for missing the bus.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing: Pattern of organizing paragraphs in essay

  • Q: Critically examine the order of arrangement of paragraphs in the text, 'Women's Role in the Pakistan Movement' and reproduce the essay by changing the pattern organisation of paragraphs to achieve your desired purpose.
    Ans: Model answer: The printed essay is arranged in chronological order: it moves from the secluded lives of women at the dawn of the twentieth century, to the Khilafat Movement (1919-1922), the Patna session of 1938, the college address of 1942, the elections and demonstrations of 1946, and the mass movement of early 1947. To change the pattern to order of importance for a speech whose purpose is to honour the greatest contribution first, the essay can be re-arranged as: (1) most importantly, Quaid-e-Azam's social revolution - women as equal partners, Fatima Jinnah at his side and the Women's Sub-Committee of 1938; (2) just as importantly, the women leaders and students who organised the cities and districts, from Jahanara Shahnawaz and Begum Fatima to the girl students who travelled to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa; (3) almost as importantly, the street struggle of 1946-47 - the Punjab demonstrations, the Peshawar session of a thousand burqa-clad women and the hoisting of the Pakistani flag on the Secretariat; and (4) finally, the background - the secluded lives from which these women rose, beginning with Bi Amma in the Khilafat Movement. The facts stay the same; only the order changes, from time order to importance order.

mcqs.q: In the printed essay 'Women's Role in the Pakistan Movement', how are the paragraphs arranged?
mcqs.why: The model answer says the printed essay is arranged in chronological order, moving through events in time sequence.

mcqs.q: Which period does the printed essay begin with?
options: The secluded lives of women at the dawn of the twentieth century
mcqs.why: The chronological essay moves from the secluded lives of women at the dawn of the twentieth century onwards.

mcqs.q: In the chronological arrangement, which event comes after the Khilafat Movement (1919-1922)?
mcqs.why: The model answer lists the order as Khilafat Movement, then the Patna session of 1938, then 1942, 1946 and early 1947.

mcqs.q: What pattern does the model answer change the essay to, for a speech honouring the greatest contribution first?
mcqs.why: To honour the greatest contribution first, the model answer re-arranges the essay in order of importance instead of time order.

mcqs.q: In the order-of-importance version, what is placed first as most important?
options: Quaid-e-Azam's social revolution, with women as equal partners and the Women's Sub-Committee of 1938
mcqs.why: The re-arranged essay puts Quaid-e-Azam's social revolution first: women as equal partners, Fatima Jinnah at his side and the 1938 Sub-Committee.

mcqs.q: In the order-of-importance version, what is placed second, as just as important?
options: The background of secluded lives only
The hoisting of the flag alone
The women leaders and students who organised the cities and districts
mcqs.why: Second come the women leaders and students, from Jahanara Shahnawaz and Begum Fatima to the girl students who travelled to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

mcqs.q: In the order-of-importance version, what is placed third?
options: The street struggle of 1946-47, including the Punjab demonstrations and the Peshawar session
mcqs.why: Third comes the street struggle of 1946-47: the Punjab demonstrations, the Peshawar session and the hoisting of the Pakistani flag.

mcqs.q: In the order-of-importance version, what is placed finally, at the end?
options: The background of the secluded lives from which the women rose, beginning with Bi Amma
The flag hoisting on the Secretariat
mcqs.why: The re-arranged essay ends with the background: the secluded lives from which these women rose, beginning with Bi Amma in the Khilafat Movement.

mcqs.q: When the paragraph pattern is changed in the model answer, what happens to the facts of the essay?
options: The facts are replaced with new facts
The facts are shortened to one paragraph
The facts are arranged by place instead
The facts stay the same; only the order changes
mcqs.why: The model answer stresses that the facts stay the same and only the order changes, from time order to importance order.

mcqs.q: What is the purpose of the re-arranged version described in the model answer?
options: To describe places in spatial order
To honour the greatest contribution first in a speech
To summarise the essay in one line
To arrange events from latest to earliest
mcqs.why: The re-arrangement is for a speech whose purpose is to honour the greatest contribution first, so importance order is used.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and speaking

  • Q: In groups of four, prepare a five minute presentation on 'Diverse roles that the Pakistani women play in various fields'. Also discuss the role of women as mothers, sisters, wives, daughters etc. and the need for them to study. Present your ideas before the class.
    Ans: Model presentation: Pakistani women play diverse roles: as mothers they raise and educate the next generation, and as sisters, wives and daughters they hold families together. Outside the home they serve as teachers, doctors, nurses, lawyers, parliamentarians, police and army officers, farmers and factory workers - just as the women of the Pakistan Movement became activists and parliamentarians. For all these roles women need to study, because an educated woman educates a whole family and, as Quaid-e-Azam taught, no nation can progress without the cooperation of its women. We should therefore support girls' education in every home.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: What are the qualities that one should have to succeed?
    Ans: To succeed, a person needs courage, strong will-power, self-confidence and self-control, together with hard work and a wise use of the abilities he has. The poem shows that success does not depend on special wealth or birth, but on determination and the resolve to say, "I can."
  • Q: How can we utilize the abilities Allah has blessed us with?
    Ans: We can utilize our abilities by using our hands for honest work, our legs to move forward, our eyes to observe and learn, and our brain to think, plan and make wise decisions. We should develop these gifts through study and practice instead of wasting them in idleness and complaint.

Comprehension A. Answer the following questions

  • Q: 1. Paraphrase the second stanza of the poem "Equipment".
    Ans: Look carefully at the wise and great people of the world. They eat their food from an ordinary, common plate, they use ordinary knives and forks like everyone else, and they tie their shoes with laces just as ordinary people do. The world calls them brave and smart, but the truth is that when they began their lives they had nothing more than you have.
  • Q: 2. Summarize the poem "Equipment".
    Ans: The poet tells a young man to think for himself: he already has everything the greatest men started with — two arms, two hands, two legs, two eyes and a brain. Great men eat from a common plate and tie their shoes with ordinary laces, so they began with no advantage over him. He can triumph and become great if he only wills it, because the man who rose to do great deeds began with no more than he has. His only handicap is himself; he must choose his place and decide how much he will learn. God has equipped him for life but leaves the choice of what to become to him. In the end, courage must come from within and he himself must furnish the will to win, so he should take hold of himself and say, "I can."
  • Q: 3. Write down the rhyme scheme of the poem "Equipment".
    Ans: The poem is written in rhyming couplets throughout. In each stanza the lines rhyme in pairs, so the scheme of every six-line stanza is AA BB CC — for example, in the first stanza: lad / had, eyes / wise, began / can.
  • Q: 4. What is theme of the poem "Equipment"?
    Ans: The theme of the poem is self-reliance and human equality: every person is born with the same basic equipment — body and brain — as the greatest men in history. Success therefore depends not on birth, wealth or special gifts, but on courage, will-power and the determination to use one's God-given abilities and say, "I can."
  • Q: 5. "All human beings are created equal". Explain this statement in the light of the poem "Equipment".
    Ans: The poem fully supports this statement. The poet says the young man has all that the greatest of men have had — two arms, two hands, two legs, two eyes and a brain — and that great men eat from a common plate and use similar knives, forks and laces. Since everyone begins life with the same equipment, no one is born superior or inferior; the difference is made only by how a person uses what God has given him.
  • Q: 6. How do you feel after reading the poem?
    Ans: After reading the poem I feel encouraged and confident. It removes every excuse for failure, because it proves that great men started with no more than I have. It fills me with hope and determination to use my abilities honestly and to face life's fight with courage, saying, "I can."

Comprehension B. Choose the correct option

  • Q: 1. The word equipment is used by the poet as __________.
    Options: simile / metaphor / personification / alliteration
    Ans: metaphor
  • Q: 2. The poem 'Equipment' by Edgar Guest is in the form of ____________, from father to son.
    Options: order / request / advice / permission
    Ans: advice
  • Q: 3. The words forks, shoes, laces are used as a _________.
    Options: imagery / alliteration / metaphor / simile
    Ans: imagery
  • Q: 4. The mood of the poem the "Equipment" is _________.
    Options: sad / ecstatic / pessimistic / optimistic
    Ans: optimistic
  • Q: 5. What according to the poem "Equipment" is essential for someone to become a great person?
    Options: Arms, hands, legs and brain / Food, common plate, forks and knives / Money, power and resources / Will, courage and self-control
    Ans: Will, courage and self-control

mcqs.q: 1. The word equipment is used by the poet as __________.
mcqs.why: The solved answer keys 'metaphor' because 'equipment' stands for the body and brain in a figurative, non-literal sense.

mcqs.q: 2. The poem 'Equipment' by Edgar Guest is in the form of ____________, from father to son.
mcqs.why: The poem is keyed as advice from father to son, urging the young man to think for himself and say 'I can.'

mcqs.q: 3. The words forks, shoes, laces are used as a _________.
mcqs.why: Forks, shoes and laces create a picture of ordinary daily life, so the book keys them as imagery.

mcqs.q: 4. The mood of the poem the "Equipment" is _________.
mcqs.why: The poem is hopeful and encouraging about using one's abilities, so its mood is keyed as optimistic.

mcqs.q: 5. What according to the poem "Equipment" is essential for someone to become a great person?
options: Food, common plate, forks and knives
mcqs.why: The book keys will, courage and self-control as essential, because everyone already starts with the same body and brain.

mcqs.q: According to the pre-reading answer, which qualities are needed to succeed?
options: Courage, strong will-power, self-confidence and self-control
mcqs.why: The pre-reading answer lists courage, strong will-power, self-confidence and self-control, together with hard work.

mcqs.q: What is the rhyme scheme of each six-line stanza of 'Equipment'?
mcqs.why: The solved answer says the poem is in rhyming couplets, so each six-line stanza follows the scheme AA BB CC.

mcqs.q: In the paraphrase of the second stanza, what do wise and great people eat from?
options: A golden plate in a palace
A special plate reserved for great men
No plate at all, only rich dishes
mcqs.why: The second stanza says great men eat their food from an ordinary, common plate, just like everyone else.

mcqs.q: According to the poem as explained in the answers, what is a person's only handicap?
options: His lack of money and wealth
His low birth and family background
His lack of arms, legs and eyes
mcqs.why: The summary says his only handicap is himself, because the difference lies in how he uses what God has given him.

mcqs.q: What is the theme of the poem 'Equipment'?
options: War and the glory of fighting
The beauty of nature in spring
mcqs.why: The solved answer gives the theme as self-reliance and human equality, since all begin with the same basic equipment.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A. Use dictionary to locate guide and entry words, choose appropriate word definition, identify pronunciation through pronunciation key: wise, laces, equipped, risen, courage, truth

  • Q: wise
    Ans: Guide words: the two words printed at the top of the dictionary page between which 'wise' falls. Entry word: wise. Definition: having or showing experience, knowledge and good judgement. Pronunciation: /waiz/ (pronounced 'wize').
  • Q: laces
    Ans: Guide words: the two words printed at the top of the dictionary page between which 'laces' falls. Entry word: lace (laces is its plural). Definition: strings or cords used to fasten shoes, drawn through holes and tied. Pronunciation: /leisiz/ (pronounced 'lay-siz').
  • Q: equipped
    Ans: Guide words: the two words printed at the top of the dictionary page between which 'equipped' falls. Entry word: equip (equipped is its past form). Definition: supplied with the things that are needed for a particular purpose. Pronunciation: /i'kwipt/ (pronounced 'i-kwipt').
  • Q: risen
    Ans: Guide words: the two words printed at the top of the dictionary page between which 'risen' falls. Entry word: rise (risen is its past participle). Definition: moved upwards; increased; got up. Pronunciation: /'rizn/ (pronounced 'riz-un').
  • Q: courage
    Ans: Guide words: the two words printed at the top of the dictionary page between which 'courage' falls. Entry word: courage. Definition: the ability to do something that frightens one; bravery and strength in the face of pain or difficulty. Pronunciation: /'kurij/ (pronounced 'kur-ij').
  • Q: truth
    Ans: Guide words: the two words printed at the top of the dictionary page between which 'truth' falls. Entry word: truth. Definition: the quality or state of being true; a fact or belief that is accepted as true. Pronunciation: /tru:th/ (pronounced 'trooth').

Vocabulary B. Write down the imagery of the poem and figure out as to what type of imagery does the poet use?

  • Q: Write down the imagery of the poem and figure out as to what type of imagery does the poet use?
    Ans: The poet creates pictures of ordinary daily life: a young man with two arms, two hands, two legs and two eyes; great men eating from a common plate with similar knives and forks; and men tying their shoes with similar laces. This is visual imagery drawn from common, everyday objects. By picturing great men in such ordinary scenes, the poet makes the reader see that greatness begins in the same simple conditions in which everyone lives.

Vocabulary C. Think over the following words and write down their connotative and denotative meaning: equipment, brain, common plate, handicap, top

  • Q: equipment
    Ans: Denotative meaning: the necessary items or tools for a particular purpose. Connotative meaning: in the poem it stands for the God-given parts and powers of the human body — arms, hands, legs, eyes and brain — with which a person is 'equipped' for the fight of life.
  • Q: brain
    Ans: Denotative meaning: the organ inside the head that controls thought, memory and feelings. Connotative meaning: wisdom, intelligence and the power to plan and decide; the poet says we have 'a brain to use if you would be wise'.
  • Q: common plate
    Ans: Denotative meaning: an ordinary plate from which food is eaten. Connotative meaning: the simple, ordinary conditions of life shared by all; even the wise and great eat from it, so it suggests equality and humility.
  • Q: handicap
    Ans: Denotative meaning: a condition that markedly restricts a person's ability to function physically, mentally or socially. Connotative meaning: in the poem, the obstacle or disadvantage a person creates for himself — 'You are the handicap you must face' — that is, his own fear, laziness and lack of will.
  • Q: top
    Ans: Denotative meaning: the highest point or part of something. Connotative meaning: the highest place in life — success, honour and greatness — as in 'start for the top and say "I can."'

Grammar A. Choose the correct preposition of movement or direction in each sentence

  • Q: 1. He goes ____ library every evening.
    Options: to / across / down / towards
    Ans: to
  • Q: 2. You must walk ____ the bridge.
    Options: into / across / down / along
    Ans: across
  • Q: 3. Walk ____ the street and turn left.
    Options: around / onto / down / across
    Ans: down
  • Q: 4. That woman going ____ the supermarket is my mother.
    Options: into / onto / across / off
    Ans: into
  • Q: 5. Sana is talking ____ Mehwish.
    Options: to / off / through / up
    Ans: to

Grammar B. Choose the correct preposition of time or place in each sentence

  • Q: 1. Stay ____ the dog. It bites.
    Options: under / to / onto / away from
    Ans: away from
  • Q: 2. Please get ____ the stage, the performance is about to start.
    Options: off / in / at / up
    Ans: off
  • Q: 3. Quick! Get the ball before it rolls ____ the hill.
    Options: in / down / up / at
    Ans: down
  • Q: 4. What do you like to do ____ the weekend?
    Options: up / in / on / to
    Ans: on
  • Q: 5. I haven't seen her ____ June.
    Options: on / since / in / for
    Ans: since
  • Q: 6. We will next meet ____ the middle of next month.
    Options: in / on / to / of
    Ans: in
  • Q: 7. Her birthday is ____ the 6th June.
    Options: at / for / on / in
    Ans: on
  • Q: 8. He was born ____ a farm.
    Options: on / between / at / to
    Ans: on

mcqs.q: 1. He goes ____ library every evening.
mcqs.why: 'To' is the preposition of movement keyed here, showing movement towards the library as a destination.

mcqs.q: 2. You must walk ____ the bridge.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'across', the preposition for moving from one side of the bridge to the other side.

mcqs.q: 3. Walk ____ the street and turn left.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'down' for moving along the street in a downward direction before turning left.

mcqs.q: 4. That woman going ____ the supermarket is my mother.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'into', showing movement to the inside of the supermarket building.

mcqs.q: 5. Sana is talking ____ Mehwish.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'to' because Sana is talking to Mehwish, directing her speech towards that person.

mcqs.q: 1. Stay ____ the dog. It bites.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'away from', warning someone to keep a distance from the dog because it bites.

mcqs.q: 2. Please get ____ the stage, the performance is about to start.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'off', meaning to leave or come down from the surface of the stage.

mcqs.q: 3. Quick! Get the ball before it rolls ____ the hill.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'down', because a rolling ball moves from the top towards the bottom of the hill.

mcqs.q: 4. What do you like to do ____ the weekend?
mcqs.why: The book keys 'on', the preposition of time used with 'the weekend' in this exercise sentence.

mcqs.q: 5. I haven't seen her ____ June.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'since', which is used with a starting point in time such as the month of June.

mcqs.q: 6. We will next meet ____ the middle of next month.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'in' in the phrase 'in the middle of next month', a fixed time expression.

mcqs.q: 7. Her birthday is ____ the 6th June.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'on', because 'on' is the preposition used before a specific date such as the 6th June.

mcqs.q: 8. He was born ____ a farm.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'on' in 'born on a farm', the place expression used in this exercise sentence.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'courage' mean in the vocabulary answer?
options: Strings or cords used to fasten shoes
Being supplied with things that are needed
The ability to do something that frightens one; bravery
mcqs.why: The vocabulary answer defines courage as the ability to do something that frightens one, that is, bravery.

mcqs.q: In the poem, what is the connotative meaning of 'common plate'?
options: A plate made of expensive metal
The simple, ordinary conditions of life shared by all
A plate used only by kings and rulers
A broken plate that cannot be used
mcqs.why: The connotation answer says 'common plate' suggests the simple, ordinary conditions of life shared by all people.

lessons.title: Language Focus (Continued)
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar: Complete the following sentences choosing the appropriate prepositional phrases

  • Q: 1. ____________ Jameel, they all seemed pretty cordial.
    Options: Except for / Except with / Except from / Except to
    Ans: Except for
  • Q: 2. ____________, cancer is curable.
    Options: To a great extent / For a great extent / In a great extent / From a great extent
    Ans: To a great extent
  • Q: 3. The train was late. ____________, I managed to get to the meeting in time.
    Options: In spite of this / In spite this / In spite to / In spite in
    Ans: In spite of this
  • Q: 4. ____________ the starter, I thought the meal was excellent.
    Options: Apart with / Apart from / Apart for / Apart to
    Ans: Apart from
  • Q: 5. What is the ____________ you?
    Options: matter of / matter with / matter on / matter to
    Ans: matter with

mcqs.q: 1. ____________ Jameel, they all seemed pretty cordial.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'Except for', the prepositional phrase used to exclude Jameel from the statement.

mcqs.q: 2. ____________, cancer is curable.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'To a great extent', the correct prepositional phrase meaning largely or mostly.

mcqs.q: 3. The train was late. ____________, I managed to get to the meeting in time.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'In spite of this', which correctly introduces a contrast with the late train.

mcqs.q: 4. ____________ the starter, I thought the meal was excellent.
mcqs.why: The book keys 'Apart from', used here to set the starter aside from the rest of the meal.

mcqs.q: 5. What is the ____________ you?
mcqs.why: The book keys 'matter with' in the fixed question 'What is the matter with you?'

mcqs.q: Which prepositional phrase from this lesson is used to exclude one person from a general statement?
options: Apart from the starter in a meal
mcqs.why: 'Except for Jameel' excludes Jameel while saying the others seemed cordial, so it marks an exception.

mcqs.q: In this lesson, 'In spite of this' is used to introduce what kind of idea?
options: A reason that explains a cause
A time that tells when something happened
A place that tells where something is
A contrast with what happened before
mcqs.why: In the train sentence, 'In spite of this' contrasts arriving in time with the train being late.

mcqs.q: Which phrase in this lesson means 'largely' or 'mostly' in 'cancer is curable'?
mcqs.why: 'To a great extent' tells the degree to which cancer is curable, meaning largely or mostly.

mcqs.q: 'Apart from' in '____________ the starter, I thought the meal was excellent' is closest in use to which idea?
options: Including the starter as the best part
Setting the starter aside from the judgement
mcqs.why: The sentence judges the meal excellent while setting the starter aside, which is the use of 'Apart from'.

mcqs.q: Which completion asks correctly about someone's problem, using a phrase from this lesson?
options: What is the matter of you?
What is the matter on you?
What is the matter to you?
What is the matter with you?
mcqs.why: The lesson's keyed phrase is 'matter with', giving the correct question 'What is the matter with you?'

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A. Paraphrase the first and last stanza of the poem 'Equipment'

  • Q: A. Paraphrase the first and last stanza of the poem 'Equipment'.
    Ans: First stanza: Think it out for yourself, my young man. You have everything that the greatest men have ever had — two arms, two hands, two legs, two eyes, and a brain to use if you wish to be wise. All great men began their lives with this same equipment, so you too should set out for the highest place and say with confidence, "I can." Last stanza: Courage must come from your own soul, and you yourself must supply the will to win. So think it out for yourself, my lad: you were born with all that the great men had, and they all began with the same equipment that you have. Take firm hold of yourself and say, "I can."

Writing B. Write in your own words the message of the poem 'Equipment' and tell how effective the message of the poem is

  • Q: B. Write in your own words the message of the poem 'Equipment' and tell how effective the message of the poem is.
    Ans: The message of the poem is that no young person should think himself unlucky or poorly gifted. God has given everyone the same equipment — a sound body and a brain — with which all great men started their lives. What a person becomes depends on his own courage, will and effort, not on his birth or wealth. The message is highly effective because it is simple, direct and encouraging: the repeated words 'Figure it out for yourself, my lad' and 'I can' stay in the reader's mind, remove his excuses, and push him to act with self-confidence.

mcqs.q: In Writing A, which stanzas of 'Equipment' are paraphrased?
options: All the stanzas except the first and last
mcqs.why: Writing A asks for a paraphrase of the first and last stanza of the poem 'Equipment'.

mcqs.q: According to the paraphrase of the first stanza, what does the young man have?
options: Only books, pens and a school bag
Nothing that great men ever had
Two arms, two hands, two legs, two eyes, and a brain
mcqs.why: The first stanza lists two arms, two hands, two legs, two eyes, and a brain to use if he would be wise.

mcqs.q: In the paraphrase of the first stanza, what should the young man say as he starts for the top?
mcqs.why: The first stanza ends with the young man setting out for the highest place and saying with confidence, 'I can.'

mcqs.q: According to the paraphrase of the last stanza, where must courage come from?
mcqs.why: The last stanza says courage must come from your own soul, and you yourself must supply the will to win.

mcqs.q: In the last stanza paraphrase, who must furnish the will to win?
options: The father who gives the advice
God, without any effort by the man
The great men of the world
mcqs.why: The paraphrase says you yourself must supply the will to win and take firm hold of yourself.

mcqs.q: What is the message of the poem, as given in Writing B?
options: A young person should wait for luck and wealth
Great men are born with special gifts others lack
Birth and wealth decide what a person becomes
God has given everyone the same equipment, so success depends on courage, will and effort
mcqs.why: Writing B says everyone has the same equipment and what a person becomes depends on his courage, will and effort.

mcqs.q: Why is the message of the poem described as highly effective in Writing B?
options: Because it is long, difficult and full of rare words
Because it is simple, direct and encouraging
Because it is sad and makes the reader give up excuses by fear
Because it praises only rich and powerful men
mcqs.why: Writing B calls the message highly effective because it is simple, direct and encouraging to the reader.

mcqs.q: Which repeated words stay in the reader's mind, according to Writing B?
options: "Figure it out for yourself, my lad" and "I can"
Wise and great people of the world
mcqs.why: Writing B says the repeated words 'Figure it out for yourself, my lad' and 'I can' stay in the reader's mind.

mcqs.q: According to Writing B, what does the message remove from the reader?
options: His arms, hands, legs and brain
His need to work and study
mcqs.why: Writing B says the message removes his excuses and pushes him to act with self-confidence.

mcqs.q: In Writing A, how does the last stanza paraphrase end?
options: With a request for more equipment from God
With a decision to wait for great men to help
With taking firm hold of yourself and saying, "I can"
With a complaint about being handicapped
mcqs.why: The last stanza paraphrase ends: take firm hold of yourself and say, 'I can.'

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and speaking

  • Q: Express your point of view, feelings, emotions and ideas about the poem Equipment in front of class.
    Ans: Model speech: Class fellows, this poem has changed the way I think about myself. Before reading it, I believed great men were born with something special that ordinary people do not have. Edgar Guest shows me this is wrong: the wise and great eat from a common plate and tie their shoes with laces like mine, and they began with the same arms, hands, legs, eyes and brain that I have. I feel hopeful and responsible at the same time — hopeful because the way to the top is open to me, and responsible because now I cannot blame anyone else. My only handicap is myself. From today I will furnish the will to win from my own soul and start for the top, saying, "I can."

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Look at the pictures and predict what the lesson is about.
    Ans: The pictures show people carrying water in containers, dry and cracked land with very little water left, and people receiving water at a distribution point. The lesson is therefore about the shortage of water — water scarcity in Pakistan — its causes, its effects on people and land, and the measures needed to save water.

Comprehension A. Answer the following questions

  • Q: 1. What are the main sources of water in Pakistan?
    Ans: The main sources of water in Pakistan are glacial and snow-melt water that rolls down the Himalayas and Karakoram, rainfall, surface water available in rivers, and underground water. The river water feeds an intricate canal system that irrigates over 16 million hectares out of 34 million hectares of cultivable land.
  • Q: 2. What are the river drainage systems of Pakistan? Describe them briefly.
    Ans: Pakistan has three river drainage basins. (i) The Indus Basin: the Indus rises near the Kailash range in Tibet, flows west and falls into the Arabian Sea; its eastern tributaries are the Ravi, Beas, Chenab, Sutlej and Jhelum, and its western tributaries are the Swat, Kabul, Kurram, Tochi, Gomal and Zhob; it gives about 141.67 million acre feet of water and is called the lifeblood of Pakistan. (ii) The closed basin of the Kharan desert: it covers the mountain basins of Quetta and the tributaries draining into the Kharan desert, such as the Pishin Lora, Baddo, Rakhshan and Mashkhel; it covers 120,100 sq. km and gives about 4.5 million acre feet from rainfall and snow. (iii) The Makran coastal basin: it consists of streams such as the Malir, Hub, Porali, Kud, Hingol, Nai, Mashhai, Dasht, Nihing and Kech; it covers 122,400 sq. km, depends on rainfall, and gives 0.78 million acre feet.
  • Q: 3. What are the main causes of water shortage in Pakistan? Discuss in detail.
    Ans: The main causes are: the construction of dams and barrages by India on the Chenab and Jhelum, which reduced Pakistan's share after the Indus Water Treaty gave the three eastern rivers to India; rapid population growth at 3.2 percent, so more than 200 million people have to be fed and supplied; non-construction of water reservoirs, because of which water worth $70 billion is thrown into the sea every year; over-pumping and wastage of underground water, which is rapidly depleting and becoming contaminated with heavy metals like copper, nickel and cobalt; very low storage capacity of only 30 days; and global warming and climate change, which further aggravate the scarcity.
  • Q: 4. What measures can we take to overcome water shortage in Pakistan?
    Ans: The lesson suggests these remedial measures: strict implementation of the National Water Policy 2018; formulation of a National Action Plan for the judicious use of available water; construction of water reservoirs; control on over-pumping of underground water and its wastage; increased use of water-efficient crops; a switch from conventional agriculture to conservative agriculture; and adopting water-efficient methods of irrigation like sprinkler and drip irrigation. In short, more reservoirs and an effective management strategy are the need of the hour.
  • Q: 5. What can you do on your own to contribute to conservation of water in your home and surrounding?
    Ans: On my own I can turn off taps while brushing teeth and washing, repair every leaking tap and pipe at home, use a bucket instead of a running hose for washing and bathing needs, and reuse leftover water for plants. I can also stop family members and neighbours from wasting water in washing cars and courtyards, and spread awareness that every drop saved today protects our future.
  • Q: 6. What is the importance of building national reservoirs? Can you point out a spot in your area where small reservoirs can be built to benefit the local population?
    Ans: National reservoirs are important because Pakistan's present storage capacity is only for 30 days, while water worth $70 billion flows into the sea every year for want of reservoirs. Reservoirs would store flood and river water for drinking, irrigation and power, recharge underground water, and protect the country from drought. In my own area, a small reservoir can be built at the low-lying spot where rainwater from the nearby hills collects and runs waste into the stream; storing it there would supply the local farms and homes in the dry season. (Any suitable local low-lying site on a seasonal stream may be named in the same way.)

Comprehension B. Choose the correct option for the following statements

  • Q: 1. Pakistan is a land where crystalline glacial water rolls down the mighty Himalaya and Karakoram peaks to the fertile land. In this sentence the phrase 'rolls down' is used as _____________.
    Options: simile / metaphor / personification / alliteration
    Ans: metaphor
  • Q: 2. Pakistan is a land gifted with lavish resources of water. By using contextual clues, the word opposite in meaning to "gifted with" is _____________.
    Options: blessed with / deprived of / bestowed with / banned upon
    Ans: deprived of
  • Q: 3. Which of the following sentences best describe the lesson 'Water Scarcity' _____________.
    Options: Conserve water and reduce its wastage / Control on over pumping of underground water and its wastage / Switch over from conventional agriculture to conservative agriculture. / Use water liberally but construct water reservoirs first.
    Ans: Conserve water and reduce its wastage
  • Q: 4. According to UNO Report, Pakistan is at ______ position in the list of countries which are facing water crisis.
    Options: eleventh / fifth / sixteenth / seventh
    Ans: seventh
  • Q: 5. After careful reading of the text, we can say that the central idea is ______.
    Options: don't make nature cry, keep your water clean / you never know the worth of water until the well runs dry / to a thirsty man, a drop of water is worth more than a sack of gold / save water to secure your future
    Ans: save water to secure your future

lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A. The following words, taken from the text, belong to the same word class. Use dictionary to find out its word class and meaning: abundant, severe, marvellous, starved, judicious, excessive

  • Q: abundant
    Ans: Word class: adjective. Meaning: existing or available in large quantities; plentiful.
  • Q: severe
    Ans: Word class: adjective. Meaning: very great or intense; (of something bad) very serious.
  • Q: marvellous
    Ans: Word class: adjective. Meaning: causing great wonder; extraordinary; extremely good.
  • Q: starved
    Ans: Word class: adjective. Meaning: suffering or dying from hunger; deprived of something needed (as in 'a water-starved country').
  • Q: judicious
    Ans: Word class: adjective. Meaning: having, showing or done with good judgement or sense.
  • Q: excessive
    Ans: Word class: adjective. Meaning: more than is necessary, normal or desirable; too much.

Vocabulary B. Change the above words into adverb and use them in your own sentences to make its meaning clear

  • Q: abundant — abundantly
    Ans: Water is abundantly available in the northern areas of Pakistan during the summer.
  • Q: severe — severely
    Ans: The whole district was severely affected by the shortage of water.
  • Q: marvellous — marvellously
    Ans: The new drip irrigation system worked marvellously and saved half the water.
  • Q: starved — (no regular -ly adverb; used in a sentence)
    Ans: Note: 'starved' does not form a regular adverb. Sentence with the word itself: The starved land cracked under the hot sun while the farmers waited anxiously for rain.
  • Q: judicious — judiciously
    Ans: We must use our underground water judiciously so that it does not run out.
  • Q: excessive — excessively
    Ans: Excessively pumping underground water lowers the water table and spoils its quality.

Grammar A. Locate the infinitives in each sentence. Identify each as an adverb, an adjective, or a noun

  • Q: 1. More than anything else, I wanted some time alone to read.
    Ans: Infinitive: 'to read' — used as an adverb (it tells the purpose for which time alone was wanted).
  • Q: 2. My grandmother told me that we have been put on earth to share, to care, to give, and to receive.
    Ans: Infinitives: 'to share', 'to care', 'to give' and 'to receive' — all used as adverbs (they tell the purpose for which we have been put on earth).
  • Q: 3. The right to vote is very valuable.
    Ans: Infinitive: 'to vote' — used as an adjective (it modifies the noun 'right').
  • Q: 4. I tried to call but the line was busy.
    Ans: Infinitive: 'to call' — used as a noun (it is the object of the verb 'tried').
  • Q: 5. To finish will be a relief.
    Ans: Infinitive: 'To finish' — used as a noun (it is the subject of the sentence).
  • Q: 6. Do you agree with the decision to go?
    Ans: Infinitive: 'to go' — used as an adjective (it modifies the noun 'decision').
  • Q: 7. To case will not be easy to solve. [as printed; read: The case will not be easy to solve.]
    Ans: Infinitive: 'to solve' — used as an adverb (it modifies the adjective 'easy').
  • Q: 8. To fly, the wings must create more lift.
    Ans: Infinitive: 'To fly' — used as an adverb (it tells the purpose for which the wings must create lift).

Grammar B. Underline the infinitive phrases in the following sentences and tell wether these infinitive phrases have been used as noun, adjective or adverb

  • Q: 1. Sending her roses is a way to win her friendship.
    Ans: Infinitive phrase: 'to win her friendship' — used as an adjective (it modifies the noun 'way').
  • Q: 2. The day to sleep in is Saturday.
    Ans: Infinitive phrase: 'to sleep in' — used as an adjective (it modifies the noun 'day').
  • Q: 3. Javed is coming to discuss the problem with the boss.
    Ans: Infinitive phrase: 'to discuss the problem with the boss' — used as an adverb (it tells why Javed is coming).
  • Q: 4. It is also possible to bring cookies rather than a cake.
    Ans: Infinitive phrase: 'to bring cookies rather than a cake' — used as a noun (it completes the meaning of 'It is also possible').
  • Q: 5. Please write the numbers to win the lottery on this form.
    Ans: Infinitive phrase: 'to win the lottery' — used as an adjective (it modifies the noun 'numbers').
  • Q: 6. The museum is fun to visit on a cold day.
    Ans: Infinitive phrase: 'to visit on a cold day' — used as an adverb (it modifies the adjective 'fun').
  • Q: 7. The captain of the ship is the authority to obey at all times.
    Ans: Infinitive phrase: 'to obey at all times' — used as an adjective (it modifies the noun 'authority').
  • Q: 8. Samia offered to think over the argument.
    Ans: Infinitive phrase: 'to think over the argument' — used as a noun (it is the object of the verb 'offered').

Grammar A. Use gerunds in the following sentences. The first one has been done

  • Q: 1. Always check the oil, before you start the car.
    Ans: Always check the oil, before starting the car. (given in the book)
  • Q: 2. The house was decorated with lights. It looked beautiful.
    Ans: Decorating the house with lights made it look beautiful.
  • Q: 3. To praise all alike is to praise none.
    Ans: Praising all alike is praising none.
  • Q: 4. I cannot go on to do nothing.
    Ans: I cannot go on doing nothing.
  • Q: 5. To collect wealth ruins health.
    Ans: Collecting wealth ruins health.
  • Q: 6. To see is to believe.
    Ans: Seeing is believing.
  • Q: 7. To give is better than to receive.
    Ans: Giving is better than receiving.
  • Q: 8. To talk like this is foolish.
    Ans: Talking like this is foolish.
  • Q: 9. She loves to read books.
    Ans: She loves reading books.

Grammar B. Underline the gerund phrases in the sentences below. The first one has been done

  • Q: 1. Brisk walking is Danial's favorite exercise.
    Ans: Gerund phrase: 'Brisk walking' (given in the book).
  • Q: 2. Mrs. Noman enjoys playing bridge.
    Ans: Gerund phrase: 'playing bridge'.
  • Q: 3. I remember promising Sami my old bike.
    Ans: Gerund phrase: 'promising Sami my old bike'.
  • Q: 4. Standing during a two-hour train trip is not my idea of fun.
    Ans: Gerund phrase: 'Standing during a two-hour train trip'.
  • Q: 5. Do you like sailing on the lake?
    Ans: Gerund phrase: 'sailing on the lake'.
  • Q: 6. Volunteering at the hospital is just one of Haleema's activities.
    Ans: Gerund phrase: 'Volunteering at the hospital'.
  • Q: 7. Mrs. Basheer enjoys watching quiz shows on television.
    Ans: Gerund phrase: 'watching quiz shows on television'.
  • Q: 8. Taking out the garbage is not my favorite job around the house.
    Ans: Gerund phrase: 'Taking out the garbage'.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A. Organize the main points of the lesson graphically with the help of mind-map and write a summary of the lesson, 'Water Scarcity in Pakistan'

  • Q: A. Summary of the lesson 'Water Scarcity in Pakistan' (main points for the mind-map: sources — Indus Basin, Kharan closed basin, Makran coastal basin; causes — Indian dams, population growth, no reservoirs, over-pumping, climate change; effects — 7th position in UNO water-crisis list, contamination, drought-like situation; solutions — National Water Policy 2018, reservoirs, drip and sprinkler irrigation).
    Ans: Pakistan is gifted with lavish water resources — glacial water, rainfall, rivers and underground water — and its three drainage basins are the Indus Basin, the closed Kharan basin and the Makran coastal basin. Yet Pakistan now faces a severe water crisis and ranks 7th in the UNO list of water-stressed countries. Indian dams on the Chenab and Jhelum, population growing at 3.2 percent, failure to build reservoirs (water worth $70 billion flows into the sea yearly), over-pumping that depletes and contaminates groundwater, storage for only 30 days, and climate change have made the shortage worse, and Pakistan may face absolute scarcity by 2025. The crisis must be taken on war footings: implement the National Water Policy 2018, build reservoirs, control over-pumping, grow water-efficient crops and adopt sprinkler and drip irrigation, because, as the lesson warns, we should save now to prevent war.

Writing B. Write a unified paragraph on the topic, 'Save a Drop Today and Reap an Ocean Tomorrow'

  • Q: B. Write a unified paragraph on the topic, 'Save a Drop Today and Reap an Ocean Tomorrow'.
    Ans: Save a drop today and reap an ocean tomorrow, because water saved drop by drop becomes the reserve that will keep our fields green and our homes supplied in the coming years. By definition, conservation means the careful, judicious use of a resource without wastage; for example, a single leaking tap can waste thousands of litres in a year, while repairing it costs almost nothing. The evidence of our own country is alarming: Pakistan has surface water of 153 million acre feet but storage for only 30 days, and it already stands 7th among countries facing a water crisis. In contrast to countries that store their river water in large reservoirs, we throw water worth $70 billion into the sea every year. This wastage causes falling water tables, contaminated groundwater and drought-like conditions in our big cities. Therefore, if every home saves its drops today — by closing taps, reusing water and adopting drip irrigation — the effect will be an ocean of water secured for tomorrow, and our future generations will thank us for it.

The Kharan, the Thar and the Cholistan basins
The Indus Basin, the closed Kharan basin and the Makran coastal basin
mcqs.why: The summary's main points list the Indus Basin, the closed Kharan basin and the Makran coastal basin as sources.

options: Absolute water abundance in all cities
An end to all water problems

options: A policy of using water liberally
A policy of pumping more underground water
mcqs.why: The summary and measures answer call for strict implementation of the National Water Policy 2018.

options: Washing cars and courtyards with running water
mcqs.why: The summary recommends adopting water-efficient methods like sprinkler and drip irrigation.

options: As using as much water as possible
As throwing river water into the sea
As the careful, judicious use of a resource without wastage
mcqs.why: The paragraph defines conservation as the careful, judicious use of a resource without wastage.

options: A running hose wastes nothing at all
A single leaking tap can waste thousands of litres in a year, while repairing it costs almost nothing
A leaking tap wastes no water in a year
Drip irrigation is only for large farms
mcqs.why: The paragraph says a single leaking tap can waste thousands of litres in a year, while repairing it costs almost nothing.

options: Pakistan has surface water of 153 million acre feet but storage for only 30 days
Pakistan stores water for a full year
Pakistan stands first among water-rich countries
Pakistan throws no water into the sea
mcqs.why: The paragraph states Pakistan has surface water of 153 million acre feet but storage for only 30 days.

mcqs.q: According to Writing B, what wastage causes falling water tables and drought-like conditions?
options: Throwing water worth $70 billion into the sea every year
mcqs.why: The paragraph links our wastage, including $70 billion of water thrown into the sea, to falling water tables and drought.

options: Fields will need no water at all
Rivers will stop flowing to the sea naturally
Future generations will have no water duties
An ocean of water will be secured for tomorrow
mcqs.why: The paragraph concludes that saving drops today will secure an ocean of water for tomorrow.

options: To describe the three river basins of Pakistan
To persuade readers to save a drop today and reap an ocean tomorrow
To list the tributaries of the Indus only
To explain how dams are built in India
mcqs.why: Writing B is a unified paragraph on 'Save a Drop Today and Reap an Ocean Tomorrow', persuading readers to conserve water.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and speaking

  • Q: Arrange a group discussion on conservation of water in your area and after conclusion of the discussion, the group leader should summerize the main points of the discussion for the benefit of the whole group.
    Ans: Model group-leader summary: Friends, our group discussed how to conserve water in our area and reached these main points. First, our area wastes most water through leaking taps, open hoses and careless washing, so every home must repair leaks and use water carefully. Second, farmers should shift from flood irrigation to sprinkler and drip methods and grow water-efficient crops. Third, rainwater should be stored in small local reservoirs and ponds instead of being allowed to run waste. Finally, we agreed that awareness is the key: if every family saves a little daily, our area can face the coming scarcity with confidence.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
A. Underline the adjective phrases in the following sentences

  • Q: 1. The main character in the story is a young boy.
    Ans: Adjective phrase: 'in the story' — it modifies the noun 'character'.
  • Q: 2. He is a visitor from another planet.
    Ans: Adjective phrase: 'from another planet' — it modifies the noun 'visitor'.
  • Q: 3. Part of the treasure map is missing.
    Ans: Adjective phrase: 'of the treasure map' — it modifies the noun 'Part'.
  • Q: 4. The road along the coastline has the best views.
    Ans: Adjective phrase: 'along the coastline' — it modifies the noun 'road'.
  • Q: 5. Several of the eggs are cracked.
    Ans: Adjective phrase: 'of the eggs' — it modifies the pronoun 'Several'.

B. Find the adjective clause in the following sentences and tell which word it modifies

  • Q: 1. I like a leader who listens to his men.
    Ans: Adjective clause: 'who listens to his men' — it modifies the noun 'leader'.
  • Q: 2. The dog which I loved dearly was hit by a truck last night.
    Ans: Adjective clause: 'which I loved dearly' — it modifies the noun 'dog'.
  • Q: 3. Rulon is a person who takes responsibility well.
    Ans: Adjective clause: 'who takes responsibility well' — it modifies the noun 'person'.
  • Q: 4. All individuals who purchased tickets will be admitted.
    Ans: Adjective clause: 'who purchased tickets' — it modifies the noun 'individuals'.
  • Q: 5. The shirt that you bought me doesn't fit well.
    Ans: Adjective clause: 'that you bought me' — it modifies the noun 'shirt'.

C. Do as directed

  • Q: 1. What is the adjective phrase in this sentence? The cabin beside the lake was already occupied when we arrived.
    Options: when we arrived / beside the lake / was already occupied / the cabin beside
    Ans: beside the lake
  • Q: 2. What is the adjective clause in this sentence? Summer, which is my favorite season, will be here in another week.
    Options: summer / will be here in another week / which is my favorite season / will be there
    Ans: which is my favorite season
  • Q: 3. What is the adjective phrase in this sentence? He finished the dish of ice cream very quickly.
    Options: of ice cream / he finished / very quickly / the dish
    Ans: of ice cream
  • Q: 4. Choose the correct option to best complete the sentence. I always remember the times __________ my cousins and I spent vacations together.
    Options: when / where / who / that
    Ans: when
  • Q: 5. Identify the phrase type in the sentence below. Houses are unbelievably expensive these days.
    Options: adjective phrase / adverb phrase / noun phrase / prepositional phrase
    Ans: adjective phrase

D. Underline the adverb phrases in the following sentences

  • Q: 1. She lives in a luxurious home.
    Ans: Adverb phrase: 'in a luxurious home' (tells where she lives).
  • Q: 2. Is there water on the moon?
    Ans: Adverb phrase: 'on the moon' (tells where the water is).
  • Q: 3. She ran into her room.
    Ans: Adverb phrase: 'into her room' (tells where she ran).
  • Q: 4. They chatted for a while.
    Ans: Adverb phrase: 'for a while' (tells how long they chatted).
  • Q: 5. She performed the task with great skill.
    Ans: Adverb phrase: 'with great skill' (tells how she performed the task).

E. Combine each set of simple sentence into one sentence containing an adverb clause

  • Q: 1. I waited for my friend. I waited till he arrived.
    Ans: I waited for my friend until he arrived.
  • Q: 2. You are intelligent. I am intelligent.
    Ans: You are as intelligent as I am.
  • Q: 3. He was not there. I left a message with his mother.
    Ans: Since he was not there, I left a message with his mother.
  • Q: 4. We wish to live. We eat for that purpose.
    Ans: We eat so that we may live.
  • Q: 5. She was very tired. She could barely stand.
    Ans: She was so tired that she could barely stand.

F. Fill in the blanks with the correct preposition (passage)

  • Q: I'm Palwasha and I live ____ Peshawar.
    Ans: in
  • Q: ____ summer I like to travel to Swat.
    Ans: In
  • Q: I like to travel ____ Swat, because of the weather and the people there.
    Ans: to
  • Q: I like to travel to Swat, because ____ the weather and the people there.
    Ans: of
  • Q: Last summer I took a bus ____ Peshawar to Swat.
    Ans: from
  • Q: ____ the bus stop we went to our hotel by taxi.
    Ans: From
  • Q: From the bus stop we went to our hotel ____ taxi.
    Ans: by
  • Q: We stopped ____ a small restaurant for a quick meal.
    Ans: at
  • Q: The driver parked the taxi ____ the restaurant.
    Ans: in front of
  • Q: Nobody could find the taxi and the driver, so we waited ____ the restaurant for one hour.
    Ans: in
  • Q: ...so we waited in the restaurant ____ one hour.
    Ans: for
  • Q: The driver was walking ____ the small park near the restaurant which we did not know.
    Ans: in
  • Q: The driver was walking in the small park ____ the restaurant which we did not know.
    Ans: near
  • Q: So we were very angry ____ him.
    Ans: with
  • Q: We sat ____ campfires and went tracking in the early mornings.
    Ans: around
  • Q: We sat around campfires and went tracking ____ the early mornings.
    Ans: in

G. Choose the correct option

  • Q: 1. Determine how the infinitive phrase is being used in the sentence. To have a balanced diet, keep the food triangle in mind.
    Options: adverb / noun / adjective / pronoun
    Ans: adverb
  • Q: 2. What is the infinitive phrase in this sentence? To surprise his family, Asad dressed up in a funny costume.
    Options: to surprise / Asad dressed up / in a funny costume / to surprise his family
    Ans: to surprise his family
  • Q: 3. Which sentence contains an infinitive phrase?
    Options: Tahir hated to leave the party so soon. / Tahir was going to a meeting. / Tahir enjoys partying with his friends. / Tahir ate cake.
    Ans: Tahir hated to leave the party so soon.
  • Q: 4. Determine how the underlined infinitive phrase is being used in the following sentence. It is also possible to bring biscuits rather than a cake.
    Options: noun / adjective / adverb / pronoun
    Ans: noun
  • Q: 5. Determine how the underlined infinitive phrase is being used in the following sentence. The day to sleep in is Sunday.
    Options: noun / adjective / adverb / pronoun
    Ans: adjective

H. Below are incomplete sentences. After each sentence are two choices to complete the sentences. One is an infinitive, and one is a gerund. Write the correct verbal in the blank

  • Q: She enjoyed ____ to you. (speaking / to speak)
    Ans: speaking
  • Q: He agreed ____ the book. (reading / to read)
    Ans: to read
  • Q: The lawyer argued for ____ the case. (dismissing / to dismiss)
    Ans: dismissing
  • Q: When they finish ____ the test, they will leave. (taking / to take)
    Ans: taking
  • Q: Are you planning ____ to the picnic? (going / to go)
    Ans: to go

I. Underline the appropriate prepositional phrase in each sentence

  • Q: 1. There are lots of birds nesting under the leaves.
    Ans: Prepositional phrase: 'under the leaves'.
  • Q: 2. After school, the children played tag at the park.
    Ans: Prepositional phrases: 'After school' and 'at the park'.
  • Q: 3. Come into the store with me.
    Ans: Prepositional phrases: 'into the store' and 'with me'.
  • Q: 4. For one hundred years the chair sat moldering in the attic.
    Ans: Prepositional phrases: 'For one hundred years' and 'in the attic'.
  • Q: 5. I gave the children eggs instead of cakes for breakfast today.
    Ans: Prepositional phrases: 'instead of cakes' and 'for breakfast'.

J. Complete the sentences with appropriate model verb

  • Q: You really ____ watch TV this much.
    Ans: shouldn't
  • Q: She ____ be at work, she always works at this time.
    Ans: must
  • Q: Speak up, I ____ hear you!
    Ans: can't
  • Q: Amir ____ call his father urgently.
    Ans: must
  • Q: Thank you for calling sir, how ____ I help you?
    Ans: may
  • Q: If I go to Peshawar, I ____ see the Bala Hisar Fort.
    Ans: will

K. Change the regular / irregular verbs in parenthesis into the past simple

  • Q: At the age of 23, she ____ (become) a doctor.
    Ans: became
  • Q: On Saturday I ____ (play) computer games with my cousins.
    Ans: played
  • Q: I ____ (know) the answer yesterday.
    Ans: knew
  • Q: He ____ (tell) me that he lived in China.
    Ans: told
  • Q: My mum ____ (not cook) dinner last night.
    Ans: did not cook

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Look at the pictures and predict what the lesson is about.
    Ans: The pictures show chickens growing much bigger between 1957 (840g), 1978 (945g) and 2005 (2202g), and a syringe being used on tomatoes. The lesson is therefore about genetically modified organisms — how scientists change the genes of plants and animals to make them grow bigger and better, and what the benefits and dangers of this change may be.

Comprehension A. Answer the following questions

  • Q: 1. What is gene and genetics?
    Ans: Genes are subunits of DNA (Deoxyribonucleic acid), the information database of an organism that is contained inside the cell nucleus; DNA carries many pairs of genes that transmit character traits of parents to their offsprings. Genetics is the study of genes, genetic variation and heredity in living organisms; it is generally considered a field of biology, but it intersects frequently with many other life sciences.
  • Q: 2. Why is the discovery of gene called a game changer in biological sciences?
    Ans: The discovery of the gene was the turning point in this field because, once genes were understood, scientists could directly change the traits of plants and animals instead of depending only on slow selection and breeding. It led to the development of genetics and genetic engineering, through which organisms with desired traits — disease resistance, larger yield and greater nutritional content — could be produced deliberately.
  • Q: 3. What is genetic engineering? What role does genetic engineering play in producing genetically modified organisms?
    Ans: Genetic engineering is the process of manipulation of an organism's genes directly by transplanting DNA from other organisms into its cells. It is the tool that produces GMOs: through it, a useful gene — for example the Bt gene for insect protection — is transferred into a crop or animal, so the resulting plant or animal carries a new desired trait that it could never get by conventional breeding.
  • Q: 4. Name some GMOs and describe their characteristics by showing how they are different from naturally occurring organisms.
    Ans: Examples from the lesson are: the Starlight Avatar, the first genetically engineered plant that glows in the dark without external stimuli because a luminescent gene from marine bacteria was introduced into the chloroplast genome of a houseplant — a natural plant cannot produce its own light; Bt crops such as cotton, potatoes and corn, which carry the Bacillus thuringiensis gene and repel insects — natural crops have no such built-in protection; fatty soya bean modified to produce less fat, and bacteria producing human insulin; glow-in-the-dark cats and transgenic cows in China engineered to produce milk containing proteins of human milk — natural cows and cats have none of these human or foreign traits.
  • Q: 5. Write at least two merits and two demerits of GMOs.
    Ans: Merits: (i) GMOs can increase food production quickly and cheaply, with crops that resist disease and insects and give larger yield and greater nutritional content; (ii) they may help eradicate many hereditary diseases and can produce useful substances such as human insulin.
