Demerits: (i) their behaviour is unpredictable — a modified crop may gain unwanted characteristics, become open to another disease, or lose nutrients such as vitamin E, and a GMO diet led to liver and kidney problems in mammals in studies; (ii) modified plants and animals may interbreed with wild populations and, through the domino effect, harm the delicate ecosystem and human health in ways that may not be known for several generations.
  • Q: 6. What in your opinion will be the effect of GMOs on our lives, life-style and environment in the future?
    Ans: In my opinion, GMOs will become a larger part of our daily food, because millions of people already purchase and eat them every day without even knowing it. Our life-style will depend more on laboratory-designed food that is cheaper and more plentiful, but if GMOs are sold without proper testing and labelling, they may quietly affect our bodies and disturb the ecosystem through interbreeding with wild plants and animals. The lesson therefore warns that the agribusiness should be profit with safety, and should slow down until the safety of GMOs is certain.
  • Q: 7. Have you ever used genetically modified foods? Give your suggestions and solutions for the safe use of genetically modified foods.
    Ans: Model answer: Like most people, I have probably eaten genetically modified food without knowing it, because GMOs are already prevalent in supermarkets and grocery stores and manufacturers are not required to label foods as having been made from GMOs. My suggestions are: every GMO should be carefully studied and properly controlled before it becomes an accepted and common practice; labelling of GMO foods should be made compulsory so consumers can choose; companies should slow down and stop selling GMOs until their safety is certain; and independent research on their long-term effects on health and the ecosystem should continue.

Comprehension B. Choose the correct option in the following statements

  • Q: 1. The information database of an organism is called _____________.
    Options: cell / genetic / genetic engineering / genes
    Ans: genes
  • Q: 2. But turning point in this field was discovery of the gene. In this sentence the phrase "turning point" means _____________.
    Options: a point in a chain of events at which an important change occurs / a point at which something rotates / a point where road branches off into two / a situation in which no change takes place in the chain of events
    Ans: a point in a chain of events at which an important change occurs
  • Q: 3. "Scientists first discovered in 1946 that DNA can be transferred between organisms". The idea expressed in this statement is based on _____________.
    Options: fact / opinion / textual inference / textual argument
    Ans: fact
  • Q: 4. After carefully reading the text "Genetically Modified Organisms", it looks to be _______.
    Options: narrative / expository / transactional / argumentative
    Ans: expository
  • Q: 5. "A few decades ago, manipulation of genes in people, plants, and animals was just science fiction". This sentence means _____________.
    Options: a few decades ago genes were multiplied and fixed in science lab with difficulty / a few decades ago the movement of genes in people, plants and animals was not as fast as it is today / a few decades ago control of genes was discussed in great detail in stories based on science / a few decades ago control of genes in living organisms seemed imaginary and was not possible in the real world
    Ans: a few decades ago control of genes in living organisms seemed imaginary and was not possible in the real world

mcqs.q: 1. The information database of an organism is called _____________.
mcqs.why: The lesson states that genes are subunits of DNA, and DNA is described as the information database of an organism contained in the cell nucleus.

mcqs.q: 2. But turning point in this field was discovery of the gene. In this sentence the phrase "turning point" means _____________.
options: a point in a chain of events at which an important change occurs
a point at which something rotates
a point where road branches off into two
a situation in which no change takes place in the chain of events
mcqs.why: Here 'turning point' is used figuratively for the moment when an important change occurs, because after genes were understood scientists could change traits directly.

mcqs.q: 3. "Scientists first discovered in 1946 that DNA can be transferred between organisms". The idea expressed in this statement is based on _____________.
mcqs.why: The statement reports a dated historical discovery from 1946, so it presents a verifiable fact rather than an opinion, an inference or an argument.

mcqs.q: 4. After carefully reading the text "Genetically Modified Organisms", it looks to be _______.
mcqs.why: The text explains and informs the reader about genes, genetic engineering and GMOs with facts and examples, which is the purpose of expository writing.

mcqs.q: 5. "A few decades ago, manipulation of genes in people, plants, and animals was just science fiction". This sentence means _____________.
options: a few decades ago genes were multiplied and fixed in science lab with difficulty
a few decades ago the movement of genes in people, plants and animals was not as fast as it is today
a few decades ago control of genes in living organisms seemed imaginary and was not possible in the real world
a few decades ago control of genes was discussed in great detail in stories based on science
mcqs.why: Calling gene control 'science fiction' a few decades ago means it then seemed imaginary and impossible in real life, although laboratories have made it real today.

mcqs.q: What are genes, according to the lesson?
options: Subunits of DNA that transmit character traits of parents to their offspring
Parts of the cell wall that protect the cell from disease
Chemicals added to crops to make them resist insects
Laboratory machines used to change an organism
mcqs.why: The lesson defines genes as subunits of DNA inside the cell nucleus, and DNA carries many pairs of genes that transmit parents' character traits to offspring.

mcqs.q: What is genetic engineering, according to the lesson?
options: The slow selection of better plants and animals for breeding
The direct manipulation of an organism's genes by transplanting DNA from other organisms into its cells
The study of heredity only through family records
The natural crossing of plants with wild populations
mcqs.why: Genetic engineering is defined in the lesson as directly manipulating an organism's genes by transplanting DNA from other organisms into its cells to produce GMOs.

mcqs.q: Why does the Starlight Avatar glow in the dark?
options: It is regularly sprayed with chemicals and ultraviolet light
Its leaves store sunlight and release it unchanged at night
It was crossed with a firefly by ordinary breeding
A luminescent gene from marine bacteria was introduced into its chloroplast genome
mcqs.why: The Starlight Avatar is a genetically engineered houseplant that glows without external stimuli because a luminescent gene from marine bacteria was placed in its chloroplast genome.

mcqs.q: What special protection do Bt crops such as cotton, potatoes and corn carry?
options: They carry extra vitamin E and never lose nutrients
They produce human insulin for diabetic patients
They carry the Bacillus thuringiensis gene and repel insects
They glow in the dark to frighten insects away
mcqs.why: Bt crops carry the Bacillus thuringiensis gene transferred by genetic engineering, which gives them built-in protection that repels insects, unlike natural crops.

mcqs.q: Which harmful effect of GMOs is reported in the lesson?
options: GMOs made chickens smaller between 1957 and 2005
A GMO diet led to liver and kidney problems in mammals in studies
GMOs stopped bacteria from producing human insulin
GMOs removed the need for labelling in supermarkets
mcqs.why: As a demerit, the lesson reports that a GMO diet led to liver and kidney problems in mammals in studies, and warns that modified organisms may also harm the ecosystem.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary: Deduce the meaning of unfamiliar words from the context by using evidence from the text and explain if you were correct, close, or totally off and why you think that happened

  • Q: breeding
    Ans: Inferred meaning: producing young plants or animals by selecting parents with desired traits — the text speaks of 'selection of better plants and animals for breeding'. Dictionary definition: the mating and production of offspring by animals or plants. Judgement: correct, because the surrounding words 'selection of better plants and animals' make the meaning clear.
  • Q: manipulation
    Ans: Inferred meaning: handling or controlling something skilfully — the text calls genetic engineering 'the process of manipulation of an organism's genes'. Dictionary definition: controlling or influencing somebody or something, often in a dishonest way. Judgement: close — the context gives the neutral sense of skilful handling, while the dictionary also carries a negative sense.
  • Q: resistance
    Ans: Inferred meaning: the power to stop something from harming — plants are developed with 'increased resistance to disease'. Dictionary definition: the ability not to be affected by something. Judgement: correct, because 'to disease' in the text points directly to this meaning.
  • Q: stimuli
    Ans: Inferred meaning: things that cause a reaction or activity — the Starlight Avatar glows 'without the need for external stimuli such as chemicals or ultraviolet light'. Dictionary definition: things that rouse activity or energy in somebody or something. Judgement: correct, because the examples 'chemicals or ultraviolet light' in the text are things that would trigger the glow.
  • Q: luminescent
    Ans: Inferred meaning: giving out light — the plant's stem and leaves 'constantly emit a faint light similar to that produced by fireflies and other luminescent organisms'. Dictionary definition: producing light without being heated. Judgement: correct, because 'emit a faint light' in the text is itself the definition.
  • Q: evaporates
    Ans: Inferred meaning: disappears or turns into vapour and is lost. Dictionary definition: (of a liquid) turns from liquid into vapour; fades away. Judgement: close — the word is a general vocabulary item practised with this table; the context of water and liquids in science writing points to the liquid-to-vapour sense.

Grammar: Classify the following sentences as declarative, interrogative, imperative or exclamatory

  • Q: 1. Yikes! I feel terrible that you got into an accident this morning.
    Ans: Exclamatory.
  • Q: 2. Where is the school?
    Ans: Interrogative.
  • Q: 3. The smoke alarm battery should be changed at least once a year.
    Ans: Declarative.
  • Q: 4. Shut that door now.
    Ans: Imperative.
  • Q: 5. I love this plant!
    Ans: Exclamatory.
  • Q: 6. Slow down before you get into an accident.
    Ans: Imperative.
  • Q: 7. How many students are in your class?
    Ans: Interrogative.
  • Q: 8. Did I say anything to make you angry?
    Ans: Interrogative.

Grammar: Rewrite the following sentences in negative, exclamatory and interrogative forms

  • Q: 1. It is kind of you to invite us.
    Ans: Negative: It is not kind of you to invite us. Exclamatory: How kind of you to invite us! Interrogative: Is it kind of you to invite us?
  • Q: 2. He is very generous.
    Ans: Negative: He is not very generous. Exclamatory: How generous he is! Interrogative: Is he very generous?
  • Q: 3. She is very knowledgeable.
    Ans: Negative: She is not very knowledgeable. Exclamatory: How knowledgeable she is! Interrogative: Is she very knowledgeable?
  • Q: 4. Gold is very precious.
    Ans: Negative: Gold is not very precious. Exclamatory: How precious gold is! Interrogative: Is gold very precious?
  • Q: 5. The wind is blowing from the west.
    Ans: Negative: The wind is not blowing from the west. Exclamatory: How fast the wind is blowing from the west! Interrogative: Is the wind blowing from the west?

Grammar: State whether the following sentences are simple, compound or complex?

  • Q: 1. The house was destroyed in the fire, but the whole family was saved.
    Ans: Compound sentence (two independent clauses joined by 'but').
  • Q: 2. Walking through the wood, he saw a fox that was following him.
    Ans: Complex sentence (it has the dependent clause 'that was following him').
  • Q: 3. The large horses walked slowly.
    Ans: Simple sentence (one independent clause).
  • Q: 4. If I do not get this job, I will start a business.
    Ans: Complex sentence (dependent clause 'If I do not get this job').
  • Q: 5. He said that he was so disappointed that he would not try again.
    Ans: Complex sentence (dependent 'that' clauses).
  • Q: 6. The men who rule the world with their pens are mightier than those who rule the world with their swords.
    Ans: Complex sentence (dependent clauses beginning with 'who').
  • Q: 7. Javed and Palwasha went home.
    Ans: Simple sentence (one independent clause with a compound subject).
  • Q: 8. The evil that men do lives after them.
    Ans: Complex sentence (dependent clause 'that men do').
  • Q: 9. All that glitters is not gold.
    Ans: Complex sentence (dependent clause 'that glitters').
  • Q: 10. Neither the colour nor the design of this cloth appeals to me.
    Ans: Simple sentence (one independent clause).

mcqs.q: What type of sentence is this: "Yikes! I feel terrible that you got into an accident this morning."
mcqs.why: The sentence expresses strong sudden feeling and begins with 'Yikes!', so in the classification exercise it is an exclamatory sentence, not a statement, question or command.

mcqs.q: What type of sentence is this: "Where is the school?"
mcqs.why: The sentence asks a direct question and ends with a question mark, so it is classified as an interrogative sentence in the grammar exercise.

mcqs.q: What type of sentence is this: "Shut that door now."
mcqs.why: The sentence gives a direct order to shut the door at once, and sentences that command or request are classified as imperative sentences.

mcqs.q: What type of sentence is this: "The smoke alarm battery should be changed at least once a year."
mcqs.why: The sentence simply states a fact or recommendation without asking, ordering or exclaiming, so it is a declarative sentence in the classification exercise.

mcqs.q: What is the negative form of "He is very generous."?
mcqs.why: The solved rewrite adds 'not' after the verb 'is' to make the sentence negative, giving 'He is not very generous' while keeping the rest unchanged.

mcqs.q: What is the exclamatory form of "It is kind of you to invite us."?
options: How kind of you to invite us!
It is not kind of you to invite us.
Is it kind of you to invite us?
mcqs.why: The solved exclamatory form begins with 'How' and ends with an exclamation mark: 'How kind of you to invite us!' expresses the same kindness with strong feeling.

mcqs.q: What is the interrogative form of "Gold is very precious."?
mcqs.why: The solved interrogative form turns the statement into a yes-no question by placing 'Is' at the beginning: 'Is gold very precious?' with a question mark.

mcqs.q: What is the negative form of "The wind is blowing from the west."?
options: Is the wind blowing from the west?
How fast the wind is blowing from the west!
The wind is blowing not from the west yesterday.
The wind is not blowing from the west.
mcqs.why: The solved negative form inserts 'not' after 'is', giving 'The wind is not blowing from the west', which negates the statement without changing its tense.

mcqs.q: State the type: "The house was destroyed in the fire, but the whole family was saved."
mcqs.why: The sentence has two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction 'but', and two independent clauses joined in this way make a compound sentence.

mcqs.q: State the type: "The large horses walked slowly."
mcqs.why: The sentence contains only one independent clause with one subject and one verb, so it is classified as a simple sentence in the exercise.

mcqs.q: State the type: "If I do not get this job, I will start a business."
mcqs.why: The sentence contains the dependent clause 'If I do not get this job' together with a main clause, and a dependent clause makes the sentence complex.

mcqs.q: State the type: "Javed and Palwasha went home."
mcqs.why: Although the subject is compound (Javed and Palwasha), there is only one independent clause and one verb, so the exercise classifies it as a simple sentence.

mcqs.q: State the type: "All that glitters is not gold."
mcqs.why: The sentence contains the dependent clause 'that glitters' inside the main clause, so it is a complex sentence according to the solved exercise.

mcqs.q: State the type: "Walking through the wood, he saw a fox that was following him."
mcqs.why: The sentence includes the dependent clause 'that was following him' describing the fox, so the solved exercise classifies it as a complex sentence.

mcqs.q: State the type: "Neither the colour nor the design of this cloth appeals to me."
mcqs.why: Despite the paired subject with 'Neither ... nor', the sentence has a single independent clause and a single verb 'appeals', so it is a simple sentence.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A. Keeping in view the text and recent advances of science, write argumentative essay on the topic "Truth Is Stranger than Fiction"

  • Q: A. Write an argumentative essay on the topic "Truth Is Stranger than Fiction", keeping in view the text and recent advances of science.
    Ans: Truth Is Stranger than Fiction. A few decades ago, manipulation of genes in people, plants and animals was just science fiction — something read in stories and never expected in real life. Today it is a reality. Scientists have produced a plant, the Starlight Avatar, that glows in the dark like a firefly because a gene from marine bacteria was placed in it; they have made cats that glow, and cows that give milk containing proteins of human milk. No novelist imagined chickens growing from 840 grams in 1957 to 2202 grams in 2005, or bacteria manufacturing human insulin, yet laboratories have done all this. Fiction is limited by the writer's imagination, but truth is limited by nothing: every year real discoveries — cloning, transgenic crops, gene therapy — go beyond what story-writers dared to invent. Some may argue that fiction predicted many inventions first, but prediction is only a guess, while science turns the strangest guesses into working facts, often in forms stranger than the guess itself. It is therefore true to say that truth is stranger than fiction, and the history of GMOs proves it.

Writing B. Search the internet about genetic modifications made in animals and write a paragraph on the first sheep ever cloned called "Molly Dolly" [as printed]

  • Q: B. Write a paragraph on the first sheep ever cloned called "Molly Dolly" [name as printed in the book; the famous cloned sheep is Dolly].
    Ans: Dolly was the first mammal ever cloned from an adult cell, born on 5 July 1996 at the Roslin Institute in Scotland. Scientists took a cell from the udder of a Finn Dorset sheep, placed its nucleus into an egg cell from which the nucleus had been removed, and implanted the resulting embryo into a surrogate mother. Out of 277 attempts, Dolly was the only lamb to survive, and she was an exact genetic copy of the donor sheep. She lived for six years, gave birth to lambs in the normal way, and proved that the genes of an adult animal could be reprogrammed to create a whole new animal — a truth that had earlier belonged only to science fiction.

mcqs.q: What is the topic of the argumentative essay in Writing A?
mcqs.why: Writing A asks for an argumentative essay on 'Truth Is Stranger than Fiction', keeping in view the GMO text and recent advances of science.

mcqs.q: Which example does the essay use of a plant made stranger than fiction?
options: The Starlight Avatar, which glows in the dark like a firefly because a gene from marine bacteria was placed in it
A tomato that ripens only under ultraviolet light in winter
A pine tree whose bark was stripped for fence posts
A sheep that was copied exactly from a donor sheep
mcqs.why: The essay says scientists produced the Starlight Avatar, a plant that glows like a firefly because a gene from marine bacteria was placed in it, proving truth stranger than fiction.

mcqs.q: According to the essay, how did chicken weight change between 1957 and 2005?
options: From 2202 grams in 1957 to 840 grams in 2005
From 945 grams in 1957 to 840 grams in 2005
From 840 grams in 1957 to 2202 grams in 2005
From 840 grams in 1957 to 945 grams in 2005
mcqs.why: The essay notes that no novelist imagined chickens growing from 840 grams in 1957 to 2202 grams in 2005, yet laboratories achieved this growth in real life.

mcqs.q: How does the essay answer the claim that fiction predicted many inventions first?
options: Fiction writers work inside laboratories with scientists
Predictions are always wrong and should be ignored completely
Science copies novels word by word without any change
Prediction is only a guess, while science turns the strangest guesses into working facts
mcqs.why: The essay concedes that fiction predicted inventions, but argues prediction is only a guess while science turns strange guesses into working facts, often stranger than the guess.

mcqs.q: What does the essay conclude about fiction and truth?
options: Fiction is limited by nothing, but truth is limited by imagination
Fiction is limited by the writer's imagination, but truth is limited by nothing
Both fiction and truth are limited by laboratory rules
Truth can never go beyond what story-writers invent
mcqs.why: The essay concludes that fiction is limited by the writer's imagination but truth is limited by nothing, so real discoveries go beyond what story-writers dared to invent.

mcqs.q: What was the correct name of the first sheep ever cloned, described in Writing B?
mcqs.why: The cloned sheep was Dolly, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell. The book prints the name as 'Molly Dolly', which is a misprint explained in the solved answer.

mcqs.q: When and where was Dolly born, according to Writing B?
options: On 5 July 1996 at a farm in Kufa
In 2005 at a laboratory in London
On 5 July 1996 at the Roslin Institute in Scotland
In 1957 at the Roslin Institute in England
mcqs.why: Writing B states that Dolly, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, was born on 5 July 1996 at the Roslin Institute in Scotland.

mcqs.q: How was Dolly produced, according to Writing B?
options: Two sheep were crossed by ordinary selection and breeding
A luminescent gene from marine bacteria was added to an egg
A cell from a tomato was joined with a sheep's egg
A nucleus from an udder cell of a Finn Dorset sheep was placed into an egg cell whose nucleus had been removed
mcqs.why: Scientists took a cell from the udder of a Finn Dorset sheep, placed its nucleus into an enucleated egg cell, and implanted the embryo into a surrogate mother.

mcqs.q: Out of how many attempts was Dolly the only lamb to survive?
mcqs.why: Writing B records that out of 277 attempts Dolly was the only lamb to survive, and she was an exact genetic copy of the donor sheep.

mcqs.q: What did Dolly's life prove, according to Writing B?
options: The genes of an adult animal could be reprogrammed to create a whole new animal
Adult animals can glow in the dark without external stimuli
Cloned animals can never give birth in the normal way
Genes cannot be transferred between different organisms
mcqs.why: Dolly lived six years and gave birth normally, proving that the genes of an adult animal could be reprogrammed to create a whole new animal.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and speaking

  • Q: Make a group comprising of five student each and discuss with each other the possible impact of genetically modified food on our future generations.
    Ans: Model discussion summary: Our group agreed that genetically modified food will feed our future generations more cheaply and in greater quantity, and may protect them from hereditary diseases. However, we were also worried: the lesson warns that altered genes behave unpredictably, that a GMO diet caused liver and kidney problems in mammals, and that modified organisms may interbreed with wild ones and disturb the ecosystem for several generations. We concluded that future generations should accept GM food only after careful study, proper control and clear labelling, so that they receive its benefits without inheriting its hidden dangers.

chapters.title: Unit 12: They Have Cut Down the Pines (By Mary Lisle)

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Discuss the title of the poem in groups and predict the content of the poem.
    Ans: The title 'They Have Cut Down the Pines' tells us that some people have felled a group of pine trees. The word 'they' suggests the poet is not one of the cutters but a sorrowful witness, so the poem is likely to be a lament: it will describe the beauty of the living pines, the loss felt by the wind, the rain, the birds and the poet herself, and the harm that cutting trees does to nature.

Comprehension A. Answer the following questions

  • Q: 1. Why were the pines cut down?
    Ans: The pines were cut down by men to make a fence by the creek — the poet says, 'They are making a fence by creek, / And have cut down the pines for the posts.' Their trunks were stripped of bark and used as fence posts, so a living grove was destroyed for a small human need.
  • Q: 2. Beside the poet, who will badly miss the company of the pines?
    Ans: Besides the poet, the wind and the rain will miss the pines — 'The wind will miss them — the rain, / When its silver blind is down.' The sun, which played hide and seek with their shadows all day, the small winds that sounded in their branches, and the bird that nested there and will now seek its home in vain, will also miss them badly.
  • Q: 3. Pick out the lines having personification.
    Ans: Lines with personification include: 'The wind will miss them — the rain' (wind and rain are given the human feeling of missing someone); 'The kind and friendly trees' (trees are given human qualities of kindness and friendship); 'And all day long the sun / Plays hide and seek with shadows' (the sun is shown playing a child's game); and 'The gentle colloquy of bough and bough' (branches are shown holding a conversation like human beings).
  • Q: 4. How has the cutting down of the tress [trees] affected nature?
    Ans: The cutting of the trees has ended the gentle conversation of bough with bough and silenced the small winds that sounded in them all day. The sun can no longer play hide and seek with their shadows, the naked trunks lie wan in the sunlight like ghosts, the brown knobby nuts are trodden into the ground, and the bird that nested there will seek its home in vain. Nature has lost shelter, shade, sound and life itself.
  • Q: 5. What picture of the rain does the words "its silver blind is down" give you?
    Ans: The words picture the rain as a fine, shining silver curtain or blind let down over the earth. When this silver blind of rain is down, the rain can no longer pass through and be broken by the pine branches as before, so it will miss the trees that once received it.
  • Q: 6. The poet mourns the cutting down of pines in a way as if she has lost her near and dear mate; why?
    Ans: The poet mourns the pines like a near and dear mate because she had lived in their living company: she calls them 'the kind and friendly trees', she had listened all day to the small winds sounding in them and watched the sun play hide and seek with their shadows. They were her companions in nature, so their felling feels to her like the death of beloved friends, not the mere removal of wood.
  • Q: 7. What is the mood of the poem and what effect does it has on you? Describe in detail.
    Ans: The mood of the poem is sorrowful, mournful and elegiac; every stanza returns to the sad refrain 'They have cut down the pines.' On me its effect is one of grief and quiet anger: I begin to see trees not as timber but as kind, friendly living companions of the wind, rain, sun and birds. It makes me feel the cruelty of destroying in a day what nature took years to grow, and it strengthens my resolve to protect trees.
  • Q: 8. What is the central idea of the poem?
    Ans: The central idea is a lament against deforestation: man carelessly cuts down beautiful, friendly trees for small selfish gains like fence posts, without caring for the loss to nature — the wind, rain, sun and birds that lived with them. The poem awakens love for trees and makes us feel that cutting them is like killing dear companions.
  • Q: 9. What are the effects of deforestation on the environment?
    Ans: Deforestation destroys the homes of birds and animals, as the nesting bird in the poem seeks its home in vain; it removes shade and shelter, disturbs rainfall and the balance of air, and leaves the land bare and exposed like the naked trunks in the poem. It also silences the natural life of a place, increases heat and soil erosion, and deprives future generations of the beauty and benefits of green forests.

Comprehension B. Choose the correct option in the following statements

  • Q: 1. And all day long the sun / Plays hide and seek with the shadows — In these lines the poet has used the literary device __________.
    Options: simile / metaphor / personification / alliteration
    Ans: personification
  • Q: 2. By using the contextual clue, the words closest in meaning to 'trodden' is __________.
    Options: trampled / walked / strolled / marched
    Ans: trampled
  • Q: 3. "The gentle colloquy of bough and bough" — In this line the poet uses the literary device _____________.
    Options: simile / metaphor / personification / rhyme
    Ans: personification
  • Q: 4. "When its silver blind is down" — In this line the phrase 'silver blind' is used as __________.
    Options: metaphor / alliteration / simile / rhyme
    Ans: metaphor
  • Q: 5. The tone of the poem is __________.
    Options: sorrowful / cheerful / wrathful / aggressive
    Ans: sorrowful

mcqs.q: 1. And all day long the sun / Plays hide and seek with the shadows — In these lines the poet has used the literary device __________.
mcqs.why: The sun is shown playing hide and seek, a human child's game, so a human action is given to the sun, which is the literary device of personification.

mcqs.q: 2. By using the contextual clue, the words closest in meaning to 'trodden' is __________.
mcqs.why: In the poem the brown knobby nuts are 'trodden into the ground', meaning crushed underfoot, so the word closest in meaning to 'trodden' is 'trampled'.

mcqs.q: 3. "The gentle colloquy of bough and bough" — In this line the poet uses the literary device _____________.
mcqs.why: Branches are shown holding a 'colloquy', that is a conversation, which is a human activity, so the line uses personification to make nature speak like people.

mcqs.q: 4. "When its silver blind is down" — In this line the phrase 'silver blind' is used as __________.
mcqs.why: Rain falling is directly called a 'silver blind' without using 'like' or 'as', comparing rain to a shining curtain, which makes the phrase a metaphor.

mcqs.q: 5. The tone of the poem is __________.
mcqs.why: Every stanza returns to the sad refrain 'They have cut down the pines' and mourns the lost trees, so the overall tone of the poem is sorrowful.

mcqs.q: Why were the pines cut down, according to the poem?
options: To build a house for the nesting bird
To make a fence by the creek, using their trunks as posts
To clear land for planting new pine trees
To make paper for the poet's books
mcqs.why: The poet says men are making a fence by the creek and have cut down the pines for the posts, so a living grove was destroyed for a small human need.

mcqs.q: Besides the poet, who will badly miss the company of the pines?
options: The fence makers and the woodcutters
The creek and the fence posts
mcqs.why: The poem says 'The wind will miss them — the rain, when its silver blind is down', so besides the poet the wind and the rain will miss the pines.

mcqs.q: What picture do the words 'its silver blind is down' give of the rain?
options: A silver window left open in a house
A blind bird flying down through the trees
A fine, shining silver curtain or blind let down over the earth
A sheet of ice covering the creek in winter
mcqs.why: The words picture rain as a fine shining silver curtain let down over the earth, which once passed through and was broken by the pine branches.

mcqs.q: What is the central idea of the poem?
options: A lament against deforestation, where man cuts friendly trees for small selfish gains without caring for nature's loss
A celebration of making strong fences from pine wood
A description of games children play in pine forests
An argument that birds should build nests on the ground
mcqs.why: The central idea is a lament against deforestation: men cut beautiful friendly trees for fence posts without caring for the loss to wind, rain, sun and birds.

mcqs.q: What will happen to the bird that nested in the pines?
options: It will build a nest on the new fence at once
It will seek its home in vain
It will sing more loudly in the remaining branches
It will fly to the creek and live in the water
mcqs.why: The poem says the bird that nested in the pines will return and seek its home in vain, because deforestation has destroyed its home completely.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary: The following words / group of words set the tone of the poem. Consult a dictionary (if required) and analyse these words and phrases to know the tone of the poem

  • Q: cut down the pines
    Ans: 'Cut down' means felled with an axe or saw. Repeated as a refrain, it sounds like a sad announcement of death, and sets a tone of loss and protest.
  • Q: wind will miss
    Ans: The wind is personified as a friend who will feel absence and grief. It sets a tone of mourning, as if the whole of nature is bereaved.
  • Q: stripped the bark
    Ans: 'Stripped' means roughly removed a covering, leaving the wood naked and exposed. It gives a tone of violence and cruelty done to a helpless living thing.
  • Q: trodden into the ground
    Ans: 'Trodden' means trampled underfoot. The brown knobby nuts crushed into the earth suggest careless destruction, adding to the tone of sorrow and waste.
  • Q: the kind, the friendly tree
    Ans: These loving words show the trees as gentle companions of man and nature. They set a tone of affection, which makes their cutting feel like the loss of dear friends.
  • Q: ended now
    Ans: 'Ended now' speaks of a final, irreversible finish — the conversation of the boughs is over forever. It deepens the tone of finality and grief.
  • Q: wan
    Ans: 'Wan' means looking pale and weak. Used for the naked trunks lying in the sunlight, it gives a tone of sickness and death.
  • Q: seek in vain
    Ans: 'In vain' means without success. The bird will search for its nest and never find it, which sets a tone of helplessness and complete loss. Together, all these words and phrases make the tone of the poem sorrowful and mournful.

Grammar A. Complete the Conditional Sentences Type I

  • Q: 1. If you (wash) __________ the dishes, I (cook) __________ dinner tonight.
    Ans: If you wash the dishes, I will cook dinner tonight.
  • Q: 2. If my dad (have) __________ time next week, we (paint) __________ my room.
    Ans: If my dad has time next week, we will paint my room.
  • Q: 3. You (learn) __________ a lot about American history if you (visit) __________ the exhibition.
    Ans: You will learn a lot about American history if you visit the exhibition.
  • Q: 4. If the weather (be / not) __________ too bad tomorrow, we (play) __________ golf.
    Ans: If the weather is not too bad tomorrow, we will play golf.
  • Q: 5. We (get / not) __________ there on time if we (catch / not) __________ the bus.
    Ans: We will not get there on time if we do not catch the bus.

Grammar B. Complete the Conditional Sentences Type II

  • Q: 1. If I (have) __________ more time, I (learn) __________ to play the guitar.
    Ans: If I had more time, I would learn to play the guitar.
  • Q: 2. If she (study) __________ harder, she (get) __________ better marks.
    Ans: If she studied harder, she would get better marks.
  • Q: 3. If we (know) __________ more about history, we (be / not) __________ afraid of the test.
    Ans: If we knew more about history, we would not be afraid of the test.
  • Q: 4. I (go) __________ jogging with Tahir and Sohail if they (be) __________ here this week.
    Ans: I would go jogging with Tahir and Sohail if they were here this week.
  • Q: 5. It (surprise) __________ me if she (help / not) __________ you.
    Ans: It would surprise me if she did not help you.

Grammar C. Finish the sentences with a clause in the correct conditional

  • Q: 1. If it is sunny tomorrow
    Ans: If it is sunny tomorrow, we will go for a picnic. (First conditional)
  • Q: 2. If you sit in the sun too long
    Ans: If you sit in the sun too long, you will get sunburnt. (First conditional)
  • Q: 3. If I were you
    Ans: If I were you, I would plant trees and protect them. (Second conditional)
  • Q: 4. If I were the Prime Minister
    Ans: If I were the Prime Minister, I would start a tree-plantation campaign in the whole country. (Second conditional)
  • Q: 5. If she had studied harder
    Ans: If she had studied harder, she would have passed the examination. (Third conditional)
  • Q: 6. If I won the lottery
    Ans: If I won the lottery, I would build a school for poor children. (Second conditional)
  • Q: 7. If I hadn't gone to bed so late
    Ans: If I hadn't gone to bed so late, I would not have felt so tired in the morning. (Third conditional)
  • Q: 8. If I hadn't come to London
    Ans: If I hadn't come to London, I would never have seen its famous places. (Third conditional)

mcqs.q: Complete the Type I conditional: "If you ______ the dishes, I ______ dinner tonight."
mcqs.why: Type I conditionals use the present simple in the if-clause and 'will' in the main clause for a real future result: 'If you wash the dishes, I will cook dinner tonight.'

mcqs.q: Complete the Type I conditional: "If my dad ______ time next week, we ______ my room."
mcqs.why: In a Type I conditional the if-clause takes the present simple 'has' and the main clause takes 'will paint' for a possible plan next week.

mcqs.q: Complete the Type I conditional: "You ______ a lot about American history if you ______ the exhibition."
mcqs.why: This Type I conditional puts 'will learn' in the main clause and the present simple 'visit' in the if-clause, expressing a real future possibility.

mcqs.q: Complete the Type I conditional: "If the weather ______ too bad tomorrow, we ______ golf."
mcqs.why: For tomorrow's real possibility, Type I uses 'is not' in the if-clause and 'will play' in the main clause: 'If the weather is not too bad, we will play golf.'

mcqs.q: Complete the Type I conditional: "We ______ there on time if we ______ the bus."
options: would not get / did not catch
will not get / will not catch
will not get / do not catch
mcqs.why: The solved Type I sentence is 'We will not get there on time if we do not catch the bus', with 'will not' in the main clause and present simple in the if-clause.

mcqs.q: Complete the Type II conditional: "If I ______ more time, I ______ to play the guitar."
mcqs.why: Type II conditionals express an unreal present wish with past simple 'had' in the if-clause and 'would learn' in the main clause.

mcqs.q: Complete the Type II conditional: "If she ______ harder, she ______ better marks."
mcqs.why: The Type II pattern uses past simple 'studied' after 'if' and 'would get' in the main clause for an imaginary improvement in her marks.

mcqs.q: Complete the Type II conditional: "If we ______ more about history, we ______ afraid of the test."
options: had known / would not have been
mcqs.why: This is Type II: past simple 'knew' in the if-clause and 'would not be' in the main clause describe an unreal present situation about the test.

mcqs.q: Complete the Type II conditional: "I ______ jogging with Tahir and Sohail if they ______ here this week."
mcqs.why: The solved Type II sentence is 'I would go jogging ... if they were here this week', using 'would go' and the subjunctive 'were' for an unreal condition.

mcqs.q: Complete the Type II conditional: "It ______ me if she ______ you." (help / not)
mcqs.why: Type II requires 'would surprise' in the main clause and past simple 'did not help' in the if-clause for this imaginary and unlikely situation.

mcqs.q: Finish correctly: "If it is sunny tomorrow, ______."
options: we would go for a picnic
we will go for a picnic
we would have gone for a picnic
we go for a picnic yesterday
mcqs.why: The solved completion uses the first conditional for a real future possibility: 'If it is sunny tomorrow, we will go for a picnic.'

mcqs.q: Finish correctly: "If you sit in the sun too long, ______."
mcqs.why: Sitting in the sun too long has a real future result, so the first conditional completion is 'you will get sunburnt', as given in the solved exercise.

mcqs.q: Finish correctly: "If I were you, ______."
options: I will plant trees and protect them
I would have planted trees last year
I would plant trees and protect them
I plant trees every day without fail
mcqs.why: The phrase 'If I were you' begins a second conditional giving imaginary advice, so the main clause uses 'would': 'I would plant trees and protect them.'

mcqs.q: Finish correctly: "If she had studied harder, ______."
options: she would have passed the examination
mcqs.why: The past perfect 'had studied' signals a third conditional about a missed past chance, completed by 'she would have passed the examination.'

mcqs.q: Finish correctly: "If I hadn't gone to bed so late, ______."
options: I will not feel so tired in the morning
I would not have felt so tired in the morning
I would not feel so tired every morning
I do not feel tired in the morning
mcqs.why: With 'hadn't gone' in the if-clause, this is a third conditional about the past, so the result uses 'would not have felt so tired in the morning.'

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing A. Paraphrase the second stanza of the poem

  • Q: A. Paraphrase the second stanza of the poem.
    Ans: They have cut down the trees, and now the gentle conversation of branch with branch has ended forever. The men are making a fence beside the creek, and for its posts they have cut down the pines. The bare trunks lie pale and weak in the sunlight like ghosts. A bird that had built its nest in these pines will come back and search for its home, but its search will be useless, because they have cut down the pines.

Writing B. Write the summary of the poem, "They Have Cut Down the Pines"

  • Q: B. Write the summary of the poem, "They Have Cut Down the Pines".
    Ans: The poet laments that men have cut down the pine trees where they stood. The wind and the rain, whose silver blind comes down through them, will miss them; their bark has been stripped from the wood and their brown knobby nuts are trodden into the ground. These kind and friendly trees, in which small winds sounded all day and with whose shadows the sun played hide and seek till night, are gone. Their gentle conversation, bough with bough, has ended, because men wanted posts for a fence by the creek. Now the naked trunks lie wan like ghosts in the sunlight, and the bird that nested there will seek its home in vain.

Writing C. Write an expository essay on "Importance of Planting Trees"

  • Q: C. Write an expository essay on "Importance of Planting Trees".
    Ans: Trees are the kindest friends of man and nature. They give us shade in the burning sun, fruit and timber for our needs, and shelter to birds and animals, as the pines in Mary Lisle's poem sheltered the nesting bird and gave the wind and sun a place to play. Trees clean the air by taking in harmful gases and giving out oxygen, they hold the soil with their roots and prevent erosion, and they attract rain and keep the climate cool and balanced. Where trees are cut down, the land becomes bare and hot, rains fail, and birds and animals lose their homes. Planting trees is therefore not a favour to nature but a duty to ourselves: every tree planted today is shade, food, rain and life for the generations of tomorrow. We should plant trees in our homes, schools, roadsides and empty lands, and protect them as we protect our own children.

mcqs.q: In the paraphrase of the second stanza, what has ended forever?
options: The making of the fence beside the creek
The shining of the sun over the creek
The gentle conversation of branch with branch
The search of the bird for food
mcqs.why: The paraphrase says the gentle conversation of branch with branch has ended forever now that the pines have been cut down by men.

mcqs.q: According to the paraphrase, why did men cut down the pines in the second stanza?
options: For posts for a fence beside the creek
For timber to build a bridge over the creek
For firewood to cook their evening meal
For clearing a road through the forest
mcqs.why: The paraphrase explains that men are making a fence beside the creek and, for its posts, they have cut down the pines in the second stanza.

mcqs.q: How are the bare trunks described in the paraphrase of the second stanza?
options: They stand tall and green in the morning light
They lie pale and weak in the sunlight like ghosts
They shine like silver blinds in the rain
They sing softly with the small winds all day
mcqs.why: The paraphrase describes the bare trunks lying pale and weak (wan) in the sunlight like ghosts after their bark and branches are gone.

mcqs.q: In the summary of the poem, whose 'silver blind' comes down through the pines?
mcqs.why: The summary says the wind and the rain, whose silver blind comes down through the pines, will miss the trees that have been cut down.

mcqs.q: According to the summary, what happened to the bark and the brown knobby nuts of the pines?
options: The bark was painted and the nuts were gathered for food
The bark was left untouched and the nuts grew into new pines
The bark was stripped from the wood and the nuts were trodden into the ground
The bark was burned and the nuts were thrown into the creek
mcqs.why: The summary records the destruction plainly: their bark has been stripped from the wood and their brown knobby nuts are trodden into the ground.

mcqs.q: According to the essay 'Importance of Planting Trees', how do trees clean the air?
options: By taking in harmful gases and giving out oxygen
By stopping all rain from falling on the land
By giving timber for houses and furniture
By providing shade in the burning sun only
mcqs.why: The essay states that trees clean the air by taking in harmful gases and giving out oxygen, which keeps the climate cool and balanced.

mcqs.q: According to the essay, how do trees prevent soil erosion?
options: They attract birds with their fruit
They hold the soil with their roots
They give out oxygen during the day
They provide timber for making fences
mcqs.why: The expository essay explains that trees hold the soil with their roots and prevent erosion, while also attracting rain and sheltering birds and animals.

mcqs.q: What does the essay say every tree planted today gives to tomorrow's generations?
mcqs.why: The essay concludes that every tree planted today is shade, food, rain and life for the generations of tomorrow, so planting is a duty to ourselves.

mcqs.q: Where does the essay advise us to plant trees?
options: Only inside forests far from towns
Only on the banks of the creek
In our homes, schools, roadsides and empty lands
Only in gardens of rich people's houses
mcqs.why: The essay urges planting trees in our homes, schools, roadsides and empty lands, and protecting them as we protect our own children.

mcqs.q: What is the main purpose of the expository essay 'Importance of Planting Trees'?
options: To explain the benefits of trees and persuade readers that planting them is a duty
To narrate the story of the nesting bird in detail
To paraphrase the second stanza of the poem
To describe how fence posts are made from pines
mcqs.why: As an expository essay it explains trees' benefits — shade, oxygen, rain, soil protection and shelter — and concludes that planting trees is a duty, not a favour.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and speaking

  • Q: Divide the class into groups of five students. Share your views in group on importance of trees and plantation. Present your argument precisely.
    Ans: Model presentation: Respected teacher and dear fellows, our group believes that trees are a lifeline of this earth and plantation is the need of the hour. Trees give us oxygen, shade, fruit and timber; they bring rain, cool the air, stop soil erosion and provide homes to birds, just as the pines gave a home to the bird in our poem. When we cut trees carelessly for small gains like fence posts, we invite heat, drought and flood. Therefore every student should plant at least one tree every year and protect the trees already standing. If we plant today, our children will breathe, eat and live tomorrow. Thank you.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: Have you ever realized that peaceful co-existence is the secret of leading a happy life?
    Ans: Yes. When people of different views, faiths and backgrounds live together with tolerance and respect, there is no quarrel, fear or hatred, and daily life becomes peaceful and happy. Hazrat Umar (R.A) ruled in this spirit: every person had easy access to him, no one was above questioning, and ruler and ruled lived without a wide gulf between them, which is why his rule is remembered for peace and justice.

A. Answer the following questions.

  • Q: 1. Why did Hazrat Umar Farooq (R.A) deposit the jewels, given by the empress of the Rome to Hazrat Umar's (R.A) wife, in the Bait-ul-Mal?
    Ans: His wife, Umme Kulsum, had sent a few bottles of perfume to the Empress of Rome, and the Empress returned the bottles filled with precious stones. Hazrat Umar (R.A) held that the gift had come to his wife only because she was the Caliph's wife, not as a private person, so it belonged to the state and not to his family. Out of honesty and integrity he therefore deposited the jewels in the Bait-ul-Mal.
  • Q: 2. Hazrat Umar (R.A) was one of those people who served the new religion with singleness of purpose. Describe the services of Hazrat Umar (R.A) to Islam in the context of this statement.
    Ans: The Rasool of Islam (PBUH) left behind a band of selfless people who dedicated themselves with singleness of purpose to the service of the new religion, and Hazrat Umar (R.A) was one of them. He was great both in war and in peace, and few persons in history have shown better qualities of head and heart. As Caliph he served Islam by ruling only for the welfare and prosperity of the people, treating the Bait-ul-Mal as a trust, keeping himself accountable before the public, and making unstinted service to humanity his foremost concern.
  • Q: 3. Humility and simplicity were the hallmarks of Hazrat Umar's (R.A) rule. Support this view by giving evidences from the given text.
    Ans: The text says his standard of living was in no case higher than that of an ordinary man: he ate barley bread and olive oil and refused wheat bread until it was available to all his people. When the Roman Emperor's envoy asked for the Caliph's palace, he was astonished to find the greatest ruler of his time lying on the bare floor of the Masjid of the Nabi (PBUH). He also called himself the people's servant, saying he had no more authority over the Bait-ul-Mal than a custodian has over the property of an orphan.
  • Q: 4. Why did Hazrat Umar (R.A) not eat wheat bread?
    Ans: When the Governor of Kufa asked why he did not take wheat bread when enough wheat was produced in his dominions, Hazrat Umar (R.A) asked whether wheat was available to each and every person in his vast dominions. The Governor replied, 'No.' The Caliph said he could not take wheat bread unless it was available to all his people, so he continued eating coarse barley bread like the poor.
  • Q: 5. How did Hazrat Umar (R.A) ensure his own accountability and the accountability of his governors before the public during his government?
    Ans: Everyone had easy access to Hazrat Umar (R.A) and every person was free to question his actions; when a man shouted in a public meeting, 'O Umar! fear Allah,' he stopped the audience from silencing him and said that if the people did not show such frankness they were good for nothing. For his governors, every Governor had to sign a bond on his appointment that he would put on coarse cloth, eat coarse bread, and that the complainant would have easy access to his presence at any time. He also insisted there should not be much distinction between the ruler and the ruled.

B. Choose the correct option.

  • Q: 1. "Hazrat Umar's (R.A) standard of living was in no case higher than an ordinary man". This shows that as caliph his lifestyle was ____________.
    Options: opulent / luxuriant / austere / lavish
    Ans: austere
  • Q: 2. Hazrat Umar (R.A) felt offended when the governor of Kufa proposed eating wheat instead of barley because ____________.
    Options: he did not like wheat / barley was his favourite food / the poor could not afford wheat / the poor did not like wheat
    Ans: the poor could not afford wheat
  • Q: 3. What according to the text was not the part of Hazrat Umar's (R.A) personality?
    Options: humbleness and simplicity / luxury and display of wealth / justice and impartiality / bravery and modesty
    Ans: luxury and display of wealth
  • Q: 4. Feeding the hungry children of the old woman is an excellent example of ____________.
    Options: humanism and social welfare of disadvantaged / political vigilance and bravery / fearlessness and courage / criminal justice
    Ans: humanism and social welfare of disadvantaged
  • Q: 5. After reading the text of the lesson "Hazrat Umar Farooq (R.A)", it can be concluded that the central point of Hazrat Umar's (R.A) rule was ____________.
    Options: welfare of people / expansion of his dominion / amassing wealth in bait-ul-mal / punishing the wrong-doers
    Ans: welfare of people

mcqs.q: 1. "Hazrat Umar's (R.A) standard of living was in no case higher than an ordinary man". This shows that as caliph his lifestyle was ____________.
mcqs.why: An austere lifestyle is simple and without luxury; Hazrat Umar (R.A) ate barley bread and olive oil and lived like an ordinary man, so 'austere' fits best.

mcqs.q: 2. Hazrat Umar (R.A) felt offended when the governor of Kufa proposed eating wheat instead of barley because ____________.
options: the poor could not afford wheat
the poor did not like wheat
mcqs.why: He refused wheat bread because it was not available to each and every person in his dominions; he would not eat what the poor could not afford.

mcqs.q: 3. What according to the text was not the part of Hazrat Umar's (R.A) personality?
mcqs.why: Humility, justice and bravery were all part of his personality, but luxury and display of wealth were not, since his living standard was never above an ordinary man's.

mcqs.q: 4. Feeding the hungry children of the old woman is an excellent example of ____________.
options: humanism and social welfare of disadvantaged
mcqs.why: Carrying flour himself at night to feed a hungry woman and her children shows care for the disadvantaged, an example of humanism and social welfare.

mcqs.q: 5. After reading the text of the lesson "Hazrat Umar Farooq (R.A)", it can be concluded that the central point of Hazrat Umar's (R.A) rule was ____________.
mcqs.why: The lesson concludes that he ruled only for the welfare and prosperity of the people, treating the Bait-ul-Mal as a trust and himself as the people's servant.

mcqs.q: Why did Hazrat Umar (R.A) deposit the jewels sent to his wife in the Bait-ul-Mal?
options: The gift had come to her only because she was the Caliph's wife, so it belonged to the state
The jewels were too heavy for his wife to wear
His wife had asked him to sell the jewels
The Empress of Rome had demanded their return
mcqs.why: Umme Kulsum received bottles filled with precious stones only because she was the Caliph's wife, so out of honesty he deposited the jewels in the Bait-ul-Mal as state property.

mcqs.q: What did Hazrat Umar (R.A) usually eat, according to the text?
mcqs.why: The text says his standard of living was never higher than an ordinary man's: he ate barley bread and olive oil and refused wheat bread until all could have it.

mcqs.q: Where did the Roman Emperor's envoy find Hazrat Umar (R.A)?
options: Sitting on a throne in his palace
Lying on the bare floor of the Masjid of the Nabi (PBUH)
mcqs.why: The envoy asked for the Caliph's palace but was astonished to find the greatest ruler of the time lying on the bare floor of the Masjid of the Nabi (PBUH).

mcqs.q: What bond did every Governor have to sign on appointment?
options: He would expand the dominion and collect more taxes
He would live in a palace and display his wealth
He would put on coarse cloth, eat coarse bread, and give every complainant easy access at any time
He would punish every complainant who questioned him
mcqs.why: To ensure accountability, every Governor signed a bond to wear coarse cloth, eat coarse bread, and keep his presence open to any complainant at any time.

mcqs.q: What did Hazrat Umar (R.A) do when a man shouted in a public meeting, 'O Umar! fear Allah'?
options: He stopped the audience from silencing the man and welcomed such frankness
He ordered the man to leave the meeting at once
He punished the man for speaking loudly
He ended the meeting and left in anger
mcqs.why: Everyone had easy access to him and could question his actions; he stopped people from silencing the man, saying people who show no such frankness are good for nothing.

lessons.title: Language Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A. Scan the text for five adjectives. Consult a thesaurus for the synonyms that are closest in meaning to the contextual meaning. Now change these synonyms into adverbs of manner and use them in your own sentences.

  • Q: Adjective from the text: simple
    Ans: Synonym closest in meaning: plain. Adverb of manner: plainly. Sentence: The teacher explained the rule plainly so that every student could understand it.
  • Q: Adjective from the text: great
    Ans: Synonym closest in meaning: grand. Adverb of manner: grandly. Sentence: The chief guest was received grandly at the school function.
  • Q: Adjective from the text: kind
    Ans: Synonym closest in meaning: gentle. Adverb of manner: gently. Sentence: She gently lifted the injured bird and placed it in a box.
  • Q: Adjective from the text: coarse
    Ans: Synonym closest in meaning: rough. Adverb of manner: roughly. Sentence: He roughly pushed the heavy door open and went inside.
  • Q: Adjective from the text: vast
    Ans: Synonym closest in meaning: enormous. Adverb of manner: enormously. Sentence: The city has grown enormously in the last ten years.

B. Form verbs from these words:

  • Q: protection
    Ans: protect
  • Q: reduction
    Ans: reduce
  • Q: initiation
    Ans: initiate
  • Q: expansion
    Ans: expand
  • Q: pleasure
    Ans: please
  • Q: food
    Ans: feed
  • Q: congratulation
    Ans: congratulate
  • Q: tight
    Ans: tighten
  • Q: response
    Ans: respond

C. The word "unique" demonstrates the following spelling rule. When using "qu" to make the "k" sound at the end of the word, add an "e". Write these words in your notebook and complete them with correct spelling of "qu" producing 'k' sound. Then use each word in a sentence.

  • Q: 1. mysti__________
    Ans: mystique. Sentence: There is a mystique about the old fort that attracts visitors.
  • Q: 2. physic__________
    Ans: physique. Sentence: The wrestler has a strong physique.
  • Q: 3. techni__________
    Ans: technique. Sentence: She has learnt a new technique of painting.
  • Q: 4. bouti__________
    Ans: boutique. Sentence: My sister bought her dress from a boutique in the bazaar.

D. Family tree

  • Q: Make your family tree and show it to your teacher/class. (A family tree starts from grandfather and grandmother, then their children, then father and mother, then their children — your siblings.)
    Ans: Model family tree (in words): Grandfather and Grandmother stand at the top. Below them come their children — my father, his brothers (my uncles) and his sisters (my aunts). Next comes my father with my mother, and below them are their children: myself and my brothers and sisters. Drawn as boxes joined by lines, the tree shows three generations: grandparents at the top, parents and their brothers and sisters in the middle, and my siblings and me at the bottom.

Grammar A. Decide whether the sentences are written in Active or Passive.

  • Q: 1. Boys like to play soccer.
    Ans: Active voice.
  • Q: 2. This room has been painted blue.
    Ans: Passive voice.
  • Q: 3. Cricket is played in Australia.
    Ans: Passive voice.
  • Q: 4. I am given a book.
    Ans: Passive voice.
  • Q: 5. We have lost our keys.
    Ans: Active voice.
  • Q: 6. You might see dolphins here.
    Ans: Active voice.
  • Q: 7. The report must be completed by next Friday.
    Ans: Passive voice.
  • Q: 8. They were singing a song in the lesson yesterday.
    Ans: Active voice.

B. Rewrite the following sentences so that the verbs will be in the active voice.

  • Q: 1. We are taught grammar by Mrs. Sikandar.
    Ans: Mrs. Sikandar teaches us grammar.
  • Q: 2. He was praised by the teacher.
    Ans: The teacher praised him.
  • Q: 3. The injured were taken to the hospital by the firemen.
    Ans: The firemen took the injured to the hospital.
  • Q: 4. The town was destroyed by an earthquake.
    Ans: An earthquake destroyed the town.
  • Q: 5. The teacher was pleased with the boy's work.
    Ans: The boy's work pleased the teacher.
  • Q: 6. The building was damaged by the fire.
    Ans: The fire damaged the building.
  • Q: 7. By whom were you taught English?
    Ans: Who taught you English?
  • Q: 8. You will be given a ticket by the manager.
    Ans: The manager will give you a ticket.

mcqs.q: The adjective 'simple' has the closest synonym 'plain'. What is its adverb of manner?
mcqs.why: In the vocabulary exercise, 'simple' is matched with the synonym 'plain', which changes into the adverb of manner 'plainly', as in explaining a rule plainly.

mcqs.q: The adjective 'kind' has the closest synonym 'gentle'. What is its adverb of manner?
mcqs.why: The exercise changes the synonym 'gentle' of 'kind' into the adverb 'gently', used in the sentence about gently lifting the injured bird into a box.

mcqs.q: The adjective 'vast' has the closest synonym 'enormous'. What is its adverb of manner?
mcqs.why: The synonym 'enormous' for 'vast' becomes the adverb of manner 'enormously', as in the sentence 'The city has grown enormously in the last ten years.'

mcqs.q: Form the verb from the noun 'protection'.
mcqs.why: The verb-form exercise changes the noun 'protection' into the verb 'protect', following the pattern of forming verbs from nouns in the list.

mcqs.q: Form the verb from the noun 'expansion'.
mcqs.why: The noun 'expansion' comes from the verb 'expand', so the correct verb form in the exercise is 'expand', meaning to become larger.

mcqs.q: Form the verb from the word 'food'.
mcqs.why: The exercise lists 'food' as a noun whose verb form is the irregular verb 'feed', as in feeding the hungry children in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Form the verb from the adjective 'tight'.
mcqs.why: Adding '-en' to the adjective 'tight' forms the verb 'tighten' in the exercise, just as other adjectives form verbs in the same list.

mcqs.q: Complete the spelling with 'qu' making the 'k' sound: mysti__________
mcqs.why: The spelling rule adds 'que' where 'qu' makes the 'k' sound at the end of a word, completing 'mysti...' as 'mystique', like 'unique' in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Complete the spelling with 'qu' making the 'k' sound: techni__________
mcqs.why: Following the 'unique' rule, 'techni...' is completed with 'que' to form 'technique', used in the sentence about a new technique of painting.

mcqs.q: Complete the spelling with 'qu' making the 'k' sound: physic__________
mcqs.why: The word is completed as 'physique' with final 'que' for the 'k' sound, used in the sentence 'The wrestler has a strong physique.'

mcqs.q: Decide the voice: "This room has been painted blue."
mcqs.why: The subject 'this room' receives the action and the verb uses 'has been painted', so the grammar exercise classifies the sentence as passive voice.

mcqs.q: Decide the voice: "Boys like to play soccer."
mcqs.why: Here the subject 'Boys' performs the action of liking and playing, so the sentence is in the active voice according to the exercise.

mcqs.q: Decide the voice: "The report must be completed by next Friday."
mcqs.why: The report receives the action and the doer is not the subject, with 'must be completed' as the verb form, so the sentence is passive voice.

mcqs.q: Rewrite in active voice: "We are taught grammar by Mrs. Sikandar."
options: Grammar is taught us by Mrs. Sikandar.
We teach grammar to Mrs. Sikandar.
Mrs. Sikandar is taught grammar by us.
mcqs.why: In active voice the doer becomes the subject: the solved rewrite is 'Mrs. Sikandar teaches us grammar', with the tense kept in the present simple.

mcqs.q: Rewrite in active voice: "The town was destroyed by an earthquake."
options: An earthquake was destroyed by the town.
The town is destroyed by an earthquake now.
mcqs.why: Making the doer the subject gives the active sentence 'An earthquake destroyed the town', keeping the past tense of the original passive sentence.

lessons.title: Writing
lessons.notes_html:
Writing

  • Q: A. Write a summary of the lesson "Hazrat Umar Farooq (R.A)".
    Ans: Hazrat Umar Farooq (R.A) was one of the selfless companions who served Islam with singleness of purpose. Born in Makkah in 40 B.H., he accepted Islam at the age of 27 and later became the second Caliph. He led a very simple life: he ate barley bread and olive oil, refused wheat bread until every person could have it, and was found by the Roman envoy lying on the bare floor of the mosque. He held himself and his governors accountable before the public, roamed at night to see the condition of his people, himself carried flour to a hungry woman and her children, and deposited in the Bait-ul-Mal even the jewels sent to his own wife. His rule was thus a model of humility, justice, honesty and service.
  • Q: B. Write a persuasive essay, having a thesis sentence, "Hazrat Umar (R.A) devoted himself to the welfare of his countrymen — not as a ruler but as a servant".
    Ans: Hazrat Umar (R.A) devoted himself to the welfare of his countrymen — not as a ruler but as a servant. He said openly, 'Brothers! I am your servant,' and declared that he had no more authority over the Bait-ul-Mal than a custodian has over an orphan's property. A servant does not eat better than those he serves: so the Caliph ate barley bread and refused wheat until it reached every home. A servant stays awake for others' comfort: so he roamed the streets of Madina at night in disguise, and when he found a mother lulling her hungry children with a kettle of water and stones, he himself carried a bag of flour three miles and cooked for them, returning the next day to apologise for his negligence. A servant also answers to his masters: he let any man question him in public and bound his governors by a signed pledge of simple living and open access. In every act, power was used as service, which is why his caliphate remains the finest example of servant-leadership.
  • Q: C. Translate the text of the incident of feeding the hungry children of the old woman by Hazrat Umar (R.A) into Urdu.
    Ans: Note: this is a translation exercise; this solved book is English-only, so no translation is reproduced here.

mcqs.q: According to the summary in Writing A, where and when was Hazrat Umar Farooq (R.A) born?
mcqs.why: The summary states that Hazrat Umar Farooq (R.A) was born in Makkah in 40 B.H., accepted Islam at the age of 27 and later became the second Caliph.

mcqs.q: At what age did Hazrat Umar (R.A) accept Islam, according to the summary?
mcqs.why: Writing A's summary records that he accepted Islam at the age of 27, after which he served the new religion with singleness of purpose.

mcqs.q: Hazrat Umar (R.A) became which Caliph, according to the summary?
mcqs.why: The summary clearly states that Hazrat Umar Farooq (R.A) later became the second Caliph, succeeding as ruler after the first Caliph.

mcqs.q: In the persuasive essay, how was the hungry mother lulling her children?
options: With barley bread and olive oil
With a bag of flour and dates
With stories about the Caliph's palace
With a kettle of water and stones
mcqs.why: The essay recounts that he found a mother lulling her hungry children with a kettle of water and stones, so he himself carried flour and cooked for them.

mcqs.q: How far did Hazrat Umar (R.A) himself carry the bag of flour for the hungry family?
mcqs.why: The persuasive essay says he himself carried a bag of flour three miles and cooked for the hungry woman and her children at night.

mcqs.q: What is the thesis of the persuasive essay in Writing B?
options: Hazrat Umar (R.A) devoted himself to the welfare of his countrymen — not as a ruler but as a servant
Hazrat Umar (R.A) expanded his dominion more than any other ruler
Hazrat Umar (R.A) collected great wealth in the Bait-ul-Mal
Hazrat Umar (R.A) lived in a palace like other kings
mcqs.why: The essay is built on the given thesis sentence that he devoted himself to the welfare of his countrymen not as a ruler but as a servant.

mcqs.q: What did Hazrat Umar (R.A) say about his authority over the Bait-ul-Mal?
options: He could spend it freely as the Caliph's personal wealth
He had more authority over it than any governor
He had no more authority over it than a custodian has over the property of an orphan
He alone could decide its use without any questioning
mcqs.why: He declared that he had no more authority over the Bait-ul-Mal than a custodian has over an orphan's property, treating public money purely as a trust.

mcqs.q: With what words did Hazrat Umar (R.A) openly call himself the people's servant in the essay?
mcqs.why: The essay quotes his open declaration, 'Brothers! I am your servant', which supports the thesis that he ruled as a servant, not as a master.

mcqs.q: What did Hazrat Umar (R.A) do the day after feeding the hungry family?
options: He punished the mother for complaining
He returned to apologise for his negligence
He ordered the Governor to resign at once
He announced a new tax in Madina
mcqs.why: After cooking for them at night, the essay says he returned the next day to apologise for his negligence in not knowing their condition earlier.

mcqs.q: How does the summary in Writing A describe his rule in its conclusion?
options: A model of humility, justice, honesty and service
A model of luxury, display and expansion
A model of strict punishment and fear
A model of wealth and palace building
mcqs.why: The summary concludes that his rule was a model of humility, justice, honesty and service, shown by his simple life and care for the people.

lessons.title: Practice Activities
lessons.notes_html:
Listening and speaking

  • Q: Consult some authentic sources from library and prepare a class presentation on the topic, "Comparison and contrast of Hazrat Umar's (R.A) administration with the present day administration of Pakistan". Present it before the class with clarity and support the topic with effective factual information.
    Ans: Model presentation: In Hazrat Umar's (R.A) administration the ruler lived like an ordinary man, ate coarse food, and could be questioned by any citizen in a public meeting; governors signed a bond to live simply and to keep their doors open to every complainant at any time, and the Bait-ul-Mal was treated as a trust, not personal property. In contrast, present-day administration in Pakistan works through elected assemblies, courts, audit and media, which are modern forms of accountability, but in practice public money is often wasted, access to high officials is difficult for a common man, and the gap between rulers' lifestyles and the people's is wide. The comparison shows that the institutions of accountability exist today, while the contrast shows that Umar's personal simplicity, direct access and fear of Allah made accountability real in daily life — the lesson our administration most needs to revive.

lessons.title: Reading and Comprehension
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

  • Q: If you were a millionaire, what would you do?
    Ans: If I were a millionaire, I would not spend all my wealth on luxury. I would build schools and hospitals for the poor, help needy students complete their education, and set up a fund for widows and orphans, because the story of Baron Hausberg shows that a true millionaire is one whose wealth removes the misery of others.

A. Answer the following questions.

  • Q: 1. What was Hughie's financial status?
    Ans: Hughie's financial status was very weak. He had once been a successful tea merchant, but a slump in the tea trade badly affected his business and he had to dismantle it. After that he tried his luck at everything but could not succeed in any business at all, and he was left with no profession except the meagre resources from his farms.
  • Q: 2. What condition was laid down by the colonel for Hughie's marriage to his daughter?
    Ans: The colonel laid down the condition that Hughie must first have ten thousand pounds of his own. Whenever Hughie's mother approached him for the marriage, he would bluntly say, 'Come to me, when your son has got ten thousand pounds, and we will see about it.'
  • Q: 3. Was Alan a good painter? What makes you think that?
    Ans: Yes, Alan Trevor was a very good painter. The text calls him a famous artist and a real master, and says his pictures were eagerly sought after. He got two thousand guineas for the single picture of the beggar-man, which shows how highly his work was valued.
  • Q: 4. Describe the role of Colonel Merton in the story. Would you describe him as a negative character or not? Why?
    Ans: The colonel is the father of Laura, whom Hughie wants to marry. He first agreed to the engagement when Hughie's tea business was thriving, but changed his mind after Hughie's repeated failures in business, and fixed the condition of ten thousand pounds. He is not truly a negative character: he is blunt and money-minded, yet his concern is practical — he wants financial security for his daughter before giving her hand to a young man with no profession and no income.
  • Q: 5. Draw the character sketch of Erskine Hughie in the story "The Model Millionaire"?
    Ans: Hughie Erskine is a handsome, soft-hearted and well-mannered young man with brown curly hair and grey eyes, popular in his circle for his good demeanour, gentle heart and unaffected plainness. He is, however, an ineffectual young man who failed in every business he tried and had only meagre resources. His finest quality is his generosity: though he himself had only a sovereign and some coppers, he gave the sovereign away to the wretched-looking beggar because, as he thought, 'he wants it more than I do.'
  • Q: 6. Describe the climax of the story in your own words. Also, present a sketch of how you would have ended the story, had you been the writer.
    Ans: The climax comes when Trevor reveals that the 'beggar' is actually Baron Hausberg, one of the richest men in Europe, and the next morning the Baron sends Hughie a cheque for £10,000 as 'a wedding present from an old beggar,' making his marriage possible. Had I been the writer, I would have ended the story in almost the same way, because the surprise rewards Hughie's kindness perfectly; I would only add a short final scene in which the married Hughie, now settled, quietly helps a poor young man as the Baron had helped him, to show that kindness passes from hand to hand.
  • Q: 7. What is the theme of the story "The Model Millionaire"?
    Ans: The theme of the story is that kindness begets kindness: generosity done from a pure heart, even to an apparent beggar and at a real sacrifice, is never wasted and returns in unexpected ways. Hughie gave away his only sovereign out of pity, and the disguised millionaire repaid that one sovereign with ten thousand pounds. The story also teaches that wealth is truly honourable only when, like the Baron's, it is used to help others.

B. Choose the correct option.

  • Q: 1. In "The Model Millionaire", what does Colonel Merton want from Hughie before he would allow him to marry his daughter?
    Options: patience / financial stability / faithfulness / commitment
    Ans: financial stability
  • Q: 2. All of these traits may be used to describe Hughie Erskine from "The Model Millionaire" except __________.
    Options: greedy / personable / handsome / unlucky
    Ans: greedy
  • Q: 3. "His pictures were eagerly sought after". In the sentence the antonym of the word "eagerly" is __________.
    Options: indifferently. / differently / enthusiastically / expectantly
    Ans: indifferently.
  • Q: 4. The theme of the story, "The Model Millionaire" is __________.
    Options: work is worship / hard work never fails / art is long but life is short / kindness begets kindness
    Ans: kindness begets kindness
  • Q: 5. In Oscar Wilde's "The Model Millionaire", Alan considered the model's face his fortune because __________.
    Options: he looked miserable / he was very poor / he looked happy / he looked serious
    Ans: he looked miserable
  • Q: 6. In Oscar Wilde's "The Model Millionaire", Baron Hausberg was interested in knowing about Hughie because __________.
    Options: Hughie was young and handsome / Hughie was jobless / Hughie was sympathetic / Hughie was arrogant
    Ans: Hughie was sympathetic

mcqs.q: 1. In "The Model Millionaire", what does Colonel Merton want from Hughie before he would allow him to marry his daughter?
mcqs.why: The colonel laid down the condition that Hughie must first have ten thousand pounds of his own, so he wanted financial stability.

mcqs.q: 2. All of these traits may be used to describe Hughie Erskine from "The Model Millionaire" except __________.
mcqs.why: Hughie is handsome, personable and unlucky in business, but he is generous, not greedy, as he gave away his only sovereign.

mcqs.q: 3. "His pictures were eagerly sought after". In the sentence the antonym of the word "eagerly" is __________.
mcqs.why: Eagerly means with keen enthusiasm, so its antonym is indifferently, meaning without interest or concern at all.

mcqs.q: 4. The theme of the story, "The Model Millionaire" is __________.
options: art is long but life is short
